subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that today the Minister of the Environment is making a very important statement on behalf of the government. I wonder if the government House leader could explain why the Minister of the Environment is not in the House of Commons, in the nation's capital,
making that ministerial statement, as opposed to elsewhere.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
I am sorry I do not have the data right here with me, but I think the hon. member will find that this government has used the House of Commons and the Statements by Ministers provisions, on orders of magnitude, more frequently than previous governments.
Indeed, I share with the hon. member the desire that this House be used more for those purposes and I encourage colleagues to do so. In fact, we do that more so by government. I would say that that, plus other changes in respect of business, in the conduct of Question Period and so on, would go a long way toward restoring the reputation of this House as the true highest court in the land.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the government that we believe it is entirely unacceptable that a document as important as this is being released this morning, at eleven o'clock, at the Bonaventure Hotel in Montreal. The House is in session. This is an important document about environmental issues. It is a long-awaited policy that had been promised by the government. I fail to see why the government treats this House with so little consideration-

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: With disdain.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
-and even with disdain, says my colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, by refusing to come here, before the members of this House, to share with us the government's environmental objectives.
Mr. Speaker, I am also amazed that the briefing notes and the minister's comments were given to others before being made available to Official Opposition critics. I think that is totally unacceptable, Mr. Speaker. The government is not playing fair, and we will not play fair with the government if it keeps playing these silly games. Ministers should realize that Official Opposition critics have the same right as friends of the Conservative Party to be advised of the government's major decisions on matters of national policy, especially concerning the

March 29, 1990
Routine Proceedings
environment. We are absolutely shocked at the arrogance shown by this government in the way it treats the Official Opposition. I think it is high time they realized that if they want consultation, if they want a House of Commons that runs smoothly, they will have to share a little with us and do so more often, and the fact that they failed to do so today in the case of a document as important as this one, on the environment, a policy that has been at least 18 months in the making and which was announced by the previous minister and the present minister-Mr. Speaker, I think that is intolerable!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, I want to take the opportunity to acknowledge what the government House leader has indicated, that in the last number of months, indeed year, we have had an opportunity to have statements on important issues presented first in the House of Commons by ministers more often than we have seen in the past.
I want to say that we have appreciated that, and we have also appreciated the courtesy that the ministers have offered the opposition spokespersons in the area of interest, in giving advance copies of the statements so there could be an informed reaction by both opposition parties. I want to say that we have appreciated that process, and that is why, I must admit, I was rather astonished this morning, knowing that this was going to be the day when perhaps the most important ministerial statement of this government is to be made.
Having not seen a written copy of this statement or, of course, not heard the statement yet, I am assuming that this is going to be the government's opportunity to actually address the critical environmental issues facing the country.
I must admit, as my hon. colleague has indicated, that we expected that to be done in the House of Commons. Again, I am simply asking, in a very serious way to my hon. friend, the government House leader, why the minister is not here in the House of Commons making such an important statement on the environment. I understand it is going to be done in Montreal. There may
be a very good reason. I am simply asking what that reason was.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. House leader of the New Democratic Party understands, in a general sense, what the reason is.
I agree with him, and I wish this place was in fact much more the focus of the national agenda than it has been. We have done a lot in the last few years to make it more so. I am sure the hon. member will understand also that because of what may be inevitable partisanship, the circus and the performances for television and so on, there is a significant disincentive to somebody who wants to get an important message out to the country.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: So, if we would be kinder to the government maybe it would make more statements.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
There is the hon. member for Glengarry- Prescott-Russell again, that great contributor to decorum in this place, the founding member of the rat pack, lecturing about how this House of Commons should be orchestrated.
The reality is that it is the rat packs of the world that detract from this place, but I welcome-I say this genuinely-that my colleague, the member for Ottawa- Vanier, feels strongly about this place and would like to see it restored to an institution where people deal with each other with respect and where the national agenda is set. In fact, if we can engage in discussions between House leaders in this regard, seek amendments to procedures, rules and so on to achieve that, I would be more than willing to participate in that activity.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to unduly delay the procedures of the House. That is not what the objective is here this morning.
Obviously, the House is concerned, members are concerned that an important issue like this has not been brought to the attention of the House. My colleagues have raised that.
However, there is a further point that I want to make to the Speaker, quite apart from the suggestions of the minister only moments ago that perhaps if members did not criticize the government so ardently, it would be
March 29, 1990

more tempted to provide information to the House. I find that unacceptable.
Beyond that, there is the further point. Not only is the statement not made in the House, it has been made a far enough distance from the House that if one wished to go there and see the press conference, members would not be able to return to Ottawa in time for Question Period.
For instance, if a member was in Montreal listening to this press conference now, it would be most unlikely that after the conclusion of the press conference, the member in question could actually come back to Ottawa in time for Question Period in order to question the government.
There are three issues: first, that it has not been tabled in the House; second, that the government has now indicated to us that the determination of the opposition toward questioning the government is a contributing factor; and finally that the government has made this decision far enough away from the Hill in order to prevent members from being here to ask questions today on the issue, either deliberately or otherwise. I am not suggesting that it is necessarily deliberately, but nevertheless the distance factor is there, and it does prevent the House from being able to be apprised of this issue, and for the issue to be questioned by hon. members today.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1990-91 ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-65
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I simply want to raise a matter as to whether or not this particular initiative has been dealt with appropriately.
First of all, I want to say I appreciate that the government House leader has been recently appointed and this is in no way criticizing what he has done this morning. He has the right to do that, I believe.
Mr. Speaker, I want to refer you to Standing Order 78(3):
A Minister of the Crown who from his or her place in the House, at a previous sitting, has stated that an agreement could not be
reached under the provisions of Sections (1) or (2) of this Standing
Order in respect of proceedings at the stage at which a public bill
was then under consideration either in the House or in any other
committee-
What this refers to in my judgment is that negotiations would take place between the parties and from those negotiations there would be an understanding that no agreement could be reached in terms of the amount of time left to require the completion of debate, recognizing the participation of all three political parties.
I recall a conversation taking place with the House Leader's parliamentary secretary who asked whether or not we could conclude this debate today. I think that was the nature of the discussion. I said that I was not certain, that we had some speakers who wanted to participate in the borrowing authority debate but I could not rightfully say whether or not we could conclude it today.
I must say that I was not under the impression that an agreement could not be reached either. I was not under the impression that we were not actually carrying on serious negotiations to see if we could not agree on an appropriate time for debate.
I simply raise this matter, Mr. Speaker, because I have a feeling that this is going to go on for some time in respect of future pieces of legislation. I simply want to ensure that before the government acts to close off debate using one Standing Order or another, that in fact the parties do sit down and attempt to negotiate an appropriate time for debate.
On this occasion I do not believe that process was completed. I think it was probably initiated, but I do not think it was completed. I do not recall any negotiations.

Which is now Standing Order 73:
-provides for a Minister to act if there is no agreement and as I stated on June 6,1988, the Chair must take a Minister's declaration at face value and cannot judge the quality of negotiations or of any proposals that may have been made.
I think that is the position that the Chair has to take.
However, I certainly can encourage hon. members, if there is still a possibility to enter into an arrangement, as the minister has suggested might be possible, then perhaps hon. members and the minister would like to discuss the matter further.

speakeroldname: Mr. Howard Crosby (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, let me begin by commenting on the necessity of the House of Commons to pass Bill C-65 in its entirety, consisting of three clauses the major thrust of which is to authorize the borrowing of $25.5 billion.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Too much. You have wasted the money we gave you last time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
The hon. member says: "Too much". I suppose he is going to argue in his presentation, when his time comes, that it should be a lesser amount. The amount arises from a calculation. The calculations are beyond dispute. There is no question about the amount. There is no question about the need and the necessity for the bill. The Financial Administration Act requires parliamentary approval of long-term borrowings. This is an annual event. If my memory serves me correctly, it has happened in some years more than once.
It is no surprise to the House of Commons that the government is presenting a borrowing bill. All administrations in the past decade or more have done the same thing, so why would the opposition be so surprised and find such need to protest this action?
Of course, members of the opposition have every right to record their concern about the massive borrowing and the massive debt of the country, but do they co-operate with the Government of Canada in a program to reduce that debt and to reduce government expenditures? No. Every day in the House they stand up objecting to this. They talk about the cuts, the clawbacks, the terrible actions taken by the government, and then when the

*

swallows come home to roost-or whoever comes home to roost-they complain.
The ultimate result of all their demands is a $25.5 billion borrowing. That does not bother members of the opposition. They object to that as well. They want to spend money. They want to spend more money than the government takes in in revenue. They do not want to increase the revenue. They do not want to borrow to support the difference. All we get is negative comment that adds up to empty rhetoric that cannot possibly convince the people of Canada that anybody on the opposite side is fit to govern this nation.
Let me talk for a minute about the national debt which is the raison d'etre for the action being taken in the House of Commons today. When the government of the right hon. Prime Minister took office in September, 1984, the national debt was $160 billion.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: What is it today?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
I want to explain that. The hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier asks what it is today. That is very easy to explain. The debt was $160 billion in September, 1984. Equally important was the fact that there was a projected deficit by the Liberal administration for that fiscal year of another $38.5 billion, totalling approximately $200 billion. That was the legacy of the Liberal government of the previous two decades. That was the legacy it left the new Progressive Conservative government-a debt of $200 billion.
I want to say to my friend, John McLeod, who writes for The Daily News of Halifax who said our claim that the national debt is $200 billion is a false claim that he did not know enough to add the projected deficit for the 1983-84 fiscal year to the accumulated debt to come up with the figure of $200 billion. It is very simple.
Members opposite say the same thing all the time. They say: "Oh, yes, you had a $200 billion debt, but why didn't you reduce it?" We did not reduce it because we did not want to destroy the social programs of Canada. We felt an obligation to the people of Canada to continue social programs and the kind of spending that
Government Orders
aids and assists the economy. We could not stop in our tracks. We were very reasonable about that.
Over the last five or six years we have made a monumental contribution to the reduction of government expenditures. We are on our way to reducing the national debt. By 1995, we will actually start to repay the national debt, something that a Liberal government would not even think of doing.
Let me tell you the facts and figures on that, Mr. Speaker. When the government of the right hon. Prime Minister took office, the projected expenditures of the Government of Canada on program expenses was $16 billion in deficit. That is to say, the revenues of Canada were $16 billion less than the projected expenditures for that fiscal year.
Four years later the government has provided for a surplus in terms of program expenditures of $9 billion. That is to say, our government will collect $9 billion more than will be spent on program expenditures. That represents a turnaround in that five-year period of $25 billion.
I would like members of the House to reflect just for a moment on what would have happened if that turnaround had not taken place by virtue of the program expenditure reductions of this government. If that initiative had not been taken and we had in addition to the current projected deficit for this fiscal year $30 billion, then we would have had an extra $25 billion to add to that deficit. We would have had a deficit of $55 billion had our government not taken the action in expenditure reduction that has been taken over the last five years.
What would happen to this country with a deficit of $55 billion? We would have the situation that exists in Brazil, Argentina and many countries around the globe where people get their pay in the morning and have to spend it that afternoon, otherwise it might be worthless that evening. There would be an inflation rate going into triple digits, not double digits as the Liberal government brought us.
These initiatives by our government are paying off and are resulting in a buoyant economy. There has been seven years of continued increase in the Gross National Product. There has been seven years of reduced unemployment. I believe, and I am from Atlantic Canada, that that is the statistic that really tells the tale.

March 29, 1990
Government Orders
We have come down in the last five years from double digit unemployment of nearly 12 per cent to an unemployment figure in 1989 of 7.5 per cent. This is something that was unheard of in the days of the budgets of Marc Lalonde and Allan MacEachen and the Liberal over spending which did not even result in effective, economic benefits in terms of employment. While the Liberal government was over spending and creating this massive debt, unemployment rose to 12 per cent in Canada. Inflation was in double digits. Every economic indicator in Canada pointed to a problem in Canada which we have set about to resolve. We have resolved it by sensible economic measures and sensible financial policy-a common sense program.
What do members of the opposition do? They obstruct every effort at improvement. Earlier today you, Mr. Speaker, saw more delay in the House of Commons. I have a little argument with my good friend from the New Democratic Party from Thunder Bay-Atikokan. In this House on March 23, 1990, he made this comment:
I would prefer if members of the Liberal party had not always caved
in to work with the government to short circuit our delaying of the
House, but so be it. That is their right.
If there was any doubt in the Speaker's mind about the necessity for bringing in time allocation and for limiting the debate on a bill, which is a common occurrence in this House, then surely that statement and other activities in this House support the absolute necessity for proceeding in this fashion.
We know that members of the opposition have no real concerns about the borrowing bill that has been presented in Bill C-65. We know members of the opposition do not intend to co-operate in some sensible way to have this measure pass so that the financial requirements can be met. Thus it is unfortunately necessary that the government has to resort to these measures to get on with the work of governing Canada and the work of ensuring financial stability for Canadians.
We are always told about reductions in social programs, the threat to social programs, but any sensible person knows that the real threat to social programs is a bankrupt national treasury. If you do not have the money in the national treasury you cannot support social programs. Anybody who demands the expenditure of more and more funds on more and more programs and loses the ability to pay for those programs is destroying our social network, not aiding and assisting that network.
I urge that all members act quickly to pass this bill to ensure that the Government of Canada has the financial ability as required by the Financial Administration Act to carry on the work of restoring economic stability to this country.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate before us flows from Standing Order 78(3). It flows from a government that does not want to have a debate on a subject matter. Therefore it cuts off debate, gags the House of Commons and imposes a limit on debate.
I want to remind Canadians who are listening here that this Bill C-65 proposes to borrow some $25 billion. We have had less than four hours of debate on the bill. Yet the government comes in and imposes time allocation on a democratic process needed to explain to Canadians what the government is going to do with that money. It will not tell Canadians what it wants to do with that money. It will not tell Canadians what the truth of the matter is, or how incompetent it is.
The truth is that this government in the last five years, in increasing economic good times, has failed to come to grips with the deficit that was just mentioned by my colleague from Halifax. Indeed, this government has doubled the deficit from what it was in 1984. It has done that even though we have had five years of international prosperity. This government has failed even to address the annual deficit, let alone the cumulative deficit of this country. It has been totally bankrupt, absolutely incapable, absolutely incompetent.
I want to tell the minister responsible for this difficult situation we are in today that the Tories' time is running out. Yet we have to accept that the majority of this House, being Tory, will have it their way. I hope Canadians will smarten up next time and not give this bunch of bandits the chance to run down debate in the House of Commons, thereby not allowing MPs of the Official Opposition and of the NDP to make comments, to ask questions, to comment positively as we usually do on the proposals put forward by the government.
March 29, 1990

I asked the minister a few minutes ago to be reasonable. I defined the word reasonable using a good dictionary, saying that it is usually used by people who are intelligent, who are willing to think a bit. Do I take it that since this minister is not reasonable that he is not intelligent and he cannot think? I am not saying that because that would be demeaning the individual. I am saying that his politics are not intelligent. I am saying to him that his methods of using a jackhammer when he could be using a smaller tool would be much more in keeping with democratic processes.
I want to address the process. Usually House Leaders, and I happen to be the one for the Liberal caucus, meet regularly with the government side to discuss the agenda of the House, to discuss House business. It usually happens on Tuesday. The minister will give us the government's plan for the coming week.
Today, this afternoon, I will ask him after Question Period what his plans are for the coming week. He will give them to us. These plans are arrived at, we hope, following consultation with all interested parties, that is, the Official Opposition and the third party.
But, Mr. Speaker, this is the thirty-fifth time in less than five years that the government has either used closure-the gagging of the House-or time allocation. Thirty-five times the government has used one of these to ram through legislation because it would not listen to debate. It would not listen to reason. It was not being very intelligent. Yet the government wonders why, today, it is at 17 per cent in the polls. I will tell the government why. It is because Canadians are saying: "We don't want you guys over there any more. You are a bunch of incompetents. You hide from us. You are secretive. You do not tell us what is going on. Yet you ram legislation through with your majority".
I ask the member from Mississauga to sit down and listen to this. I am telling him that someday he will regret being associated with that bunch of people he calls his friends in the Tory party. He is a nice fellow, and I have nothing against him. It is the gang he hangs around with that I cannot stand. They have absolutely no understanding of what the process is all about or what democracy is all about.

I say the same thing to the member for Halifax West. I like the guy. He is a nice fellow, but he too hangs around with the wrong gang. He will have to account to the taxpayers come the next election. He will be very sorry to hear them say: "We don't want you any more, Howard". That is going to be the message they are going to have to give this fellow.
Do you know why, Mr. Speaker? Because they have been absolutely incompetent in coming to grips with the problems of this country. They have been unable to work with the House of Commons. Even though the government has a massive majority, it has been unable to come to us in a reasonable fashion to put reasonable things before the House. They have been unable to do as reasonable people do, that is, debate. Normally, after a reasonable debate, the question is put.
I am a very reasonable man, and even the minister will admit that. I want to negotiate time allocation if we have to, but within another a specific order. If he needs to have certain legislation, we have always said that we would co-operate.
The hon. member from Halifax West mentioned co-operate in his comments. He said that we did not co-operate.

In French, to co-operate means to operate with someone. Mr. Speaker, that is what we want to do with the government. We want to try and help them out of the present morass. We want to help these poor Tory members regain some of the pride they had in belonging to a big party that is now sadly crumbling. With 17 per cent of support in the polls, Mr. Speaker, this means not one of them would be re-elected if an election were held tomorrow. That is the truth, Mr. Speaker. And there they are, wielding a big stick, imposing closure and time allocation and telling members: we don't want to listen to sensible arguments, we don't want to listen to a democratic debate. We only want to end the debate, gag the House of Commons and impose our ideas, our ideology.
Mr. Speaker, about the mushrooming deficit referred to by the hon. member for Halifax, the Minister of Finance, when he was elected, announced a five-year plan that would reduce taxes by half by at the end of that period. Well, Mr. Speaker, he failed to keep that promise as well. Today, the federal deficit has doubled. In 1984 it was $170 billion, and today it is $351 billion. Mr. Speaker, with all due respect for the Tory caucus and all the Tory

ministers, they started their fight against the deficit in 1984, at a time when we were in good shape and the international economy was in good shape, but the government failed to reduce the deficit in five years. The deficit is certainly not less than it was in 1984. And I ask you why, since they taxed Canadians 31 times, in the form of 31 additional taxes in five years, why none of this was able to absorb the national debt? Why? Because they are incompetent and entirely incapable of running this country, and it is high time we got rid of them, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I must say that there are dark, evil and sinister forces at work in the House at this moment.
I look across the aisle and I see Conservative members as individuals. They are very decent people. But something happens when they get together. They start thinking in terms of totalitarianism or dictatorial initiatives; and they do not like to hear dissent. They do not like to hear people saying that they are doing the wrong thing.
Let us understand what is happening at this moment. The government decided, because it has mismanaged the economy so badly, that it had to bring in a special bill, Bill C-65, to ask permission to borrow vast sums of money. It is not hundreds of millions, or a billion dollars, but billions and billions of dollars, $25.5 billion. Can you imagine what the interest on $25.5 billion is going to cost the taxpayers of this country because of the mismanagement of the government?
The bankers love the Tories because they know that they are going to rack up the biggest debts and deficits ever seen or imagined in this country. The bankers say: "We thought the Liberals were bad, but my goodness the Tories doubled their debts".
Let us look back at what this government has done. It introduced this bill and then said: "Listen, we have to pull a quickie here because if the people of Canada realize what we are doing, they are going to get awfully upset, so we are not going to allow any debate on this bill". Can you imagine not allowing any debate on a bill that requests the borrowing authority for $25.5 billion? That is what the government says. "We do not want to hear any opposition. We do not want to hear any
criticisms of what we are doing or this incredible debt load we are about to impose on the young people of this country". So it brought in a form of closure which is a totalitarian tactic that this government now has introduced time and time again because it does not like opposition members telling the truth.
The government does not like people telling the truth. The other day there was a poor priest out in front of the Parliament Buildings. I might disagree with the cause that he represents but he has the right to stand in front of his Parliament Buildings with a small plaque outlying the cause of his concern. He has a right to do that because this Parliament does not belong to the Conservative party. This is not the Conservative government's Parliament. This is the people of Canada's Parliament.
The priest was quietly standing there day after day as his way of protesting what he thought the government was doing and to suggest to members what he thought that they should do. What does the government do? It passes a law in secret and then brings in the police to drag this poor priest down to the jail, throw him behind bars and clank the doors dosed, and he sits there for days and days in shackles, my hon. friend from Edmonton tells me. All this person did was stand in front of his Parliament, quietly, day after day. He was released from jail and now he is going to be going to court. Presumably he will be found guilty. I do not want to presume that but I suppose if the law that the government brought in is enforced, which everybody now agrees is a totally silly, oppressive law that ought not to occur in a democratic country, he will be found guilty and have to pay a fine presumably, to say nothing of others who were also arrested.
Why does the government want to do business in secret? Why does it want to do business behind closed doors? Why does it not want people to know what it is doing? Why does it not want to allow opposition members to voice their concerns? No wonder people are cynical about the government. No wonder the people of Canada do not trust the government, because it does not allow the free expression of people's views in this country. It is a very totalitarian approach, just as the East Bloc countries are opening up their systems and stating that they welcome dissent, and welcome people grouping together to express their views and indicate alternatives. While the East Bloc countries are lifting off the shackles, here they are shackling priests and throwing them in jail

for doing nothing more than simply standing in front of the precincts of Parliament.
There is something sinister about this process. We just cannot stand here and say that there is nothing we can do about this; this is something that is appropriate. It almost makes one gasp when looking at the record.
Back in 1979 the government decided to use some form of closure twice. In 1980, when there seemed to be an impasse, the government decided to use closure once to get their legislation through. Goodness knows, at the end of the day, after considerable debate, the government has the right to pass legislation, but only after reasonable debate.
In 1981 there was one effort to muzzle off the Parliament of Canada. In 1984, it was used twice. Then the Conservatives were elected and time after time closure was used. In the report I received from the Library just a few minutes ago on statistics respecting House business, we find that in the last 11 months, time allocation or closure was used a total of 15 times.
This is a government that does not like freedom of expression. This is a government that does not like freedom of speech. This is a government that does not recognize the traditions, practices and customs of Parliament. It does not recognize that there is an opposition. We have an obligation to Her Majesty to oppose and critique government legislation. That is our job. We are paid to do that, and the government will not let us do that.
Look at the times the government has closed off debate in the House of Commons, the last place where the elected representatives of the people of Canada can express their views. This is the way it has been done for decades, in excess of 100 years. This is the way it has been done in the Mother of Parliaments for hundreds of years. Yet this is the only government in Canadian history that has used closure and closure and closure, time after time and it is accelerating.
If the people of Canada really knew what was going on, they would probably be revolting. They would find what is going on revolting, and they in turn would revolt. The government is going to borrow, on their behalf, $25

billion. What is worse is that this afternoon the interest rates are probably going to go up, which means billions of dollars in additional interest rate payments will be paid by our children as a result of this government initiative, and after only a handful of hours of debate on one of the largest borrowing authorities in Canadian history the government states that it is not going to tolerate any more debate. That is wrong. It is undemocratic. There is no place in a parliamentary institution, after that length of time, for the government to muzzle debate. Had the debate on this borrowing authority for $25.5 billion gone on for a week or two I can see then the government stating that it is time to move this legislation to the next stage.
Is there a single Conservative member opposite, and I look at my hon. friend, the chairman of the cultural committee, who is prepared to stand up in this House and say: "I believe that after a handful of hours, one day debate, it is time for the government House leader to muzzle off the Parliament of Canada." Yet, that is exactly what is going on.
In another hour and a half we are going to vote on this. I really hope that any member who rises in this House to support this muzzling of Parliament, this closing off debate at this stage of the largest borrowing authority in Canadian history and part of a process which we have never seen before in terms of being so anti-democratic, will think before they support this legislation.
Let's recognize that eventually the sides are going to switch in this House. Members opposite can be smug and say: "We are in government now and we can do anything we want." That is not the way the parliamentary system works. This is not a four year dictatorship that we have in this country. There is a role for the opposition parties. Unfortunately it has become a four year dictatorship, but the parliamentary system requires that legislation be debated. That is why we are here. It is our job to debate legislation. But to debate legislation, we must have time. We must have the opportunity to do that.

That is why I appeal to those members on the government side when the time comes to vote, please vote for freedom of speech. Vote for democracy and vote to uphold our traditions of Parliament that we dearly love.

Mr. Speaker, it certainly must be Thursday noon because of what I am hearing from my hon. colleagues from the New Democratic Party this morning in the debate on this borrowing authority which the government seeks. I find what I heard this morning absolutely unbelievable.
I seem to recall a few days ago sitting in the finance committee when the very party criticizing this government for restricting debate, filibustered real debate for 30 hours on the finance committee considering the proposed goods and services tax. They really filibustered and talked about every kind of nonsense, what Canadians were not at all thinking about, and now accuse us of restricting debate. When proper debating times were given and accorded the opposition party, they were the ones who filibustered.
They stand here today screaming about the authority to borrow this money, which goes into the financing the debt, and nobody denies that there is a tremendous debt, but also funding programs. These are the very programs that the New Democratic Party always says are too little, too late. For the last six years, every time a New Democrat stood up in the House of Commons, he or she said the government did not spend enough money on a program, whether it was agriculture or whatever. When the government spent a billion, they stood up and said it is too little, too late. They would have spent $2 billion.
The fact is that the money we are trying to borrow to run this country would never have been enough for members of the New Democratic Party. They would have had to borrow $50 billion because they speak out of both sides of their mouths. They are saying we should debate the amount we are borrowing and yet I have heard for six years that whatever we did, whatever program, we never spent enough money.
Where do they really stand on the issue of financing government projects? Do they want the government to spend more on these programs, in which case there has to be revenue, in which case there has to be borrowing
authority. On the other hand, do they want to reduce these programs? I do not think any one member of the New Democratic Party could stand in the House today and persuade any Canadian to vote for them if they would reduce programs.
In fact, the very bill that we are debating is a money bill. It is a requirement of funds for programs to finance debt. Every one of them knows that prior to 1984 when the Liberals were in power, they supported the ridiculous spending programs of the Liberal party, knowing that some day Canadians would have to pay. That is exactly what is happening today. The biggest portion of our debt since 1984 is moneys to pay back former debt which is almost $100 billion or $120 billion. They do not want to stand and talk about it because even the New Democratic Party was responsible for that debt.
When we hear the hon. members from that party stand in their place and say the government gives too little, too late, there is not enough for agriculture, not enough for seniors, not enough for this and not enough for that, what they are saying to Canadians is that we should borrow more money. We should actually borrow billions more, as they were used to with their colleagues. That is what has happened and what has been suggested.
Even members of the Liberal party have stood up in their places since 1984 and said that the government has not provided enough money for programs for Canadians. That is the way of the past. There is going to be a fear as we approach the next election that that old group, the old team is going to revert back to the style of borrow, borrow, spend, spend. There will be no conscious effort to reduce the deficit as we are seeing the Minister of Finance do. They never talk that way. I recall vividly during the last campaign that the then leader of the Liberal party suggested that they were going to reduce the deficit. Yes, that was the plan. They had no way of achieving that, but that is what they had a plan for. I suppose if you were to really investigate the New Democratic's platform, somewhere hidden in small print for a specific audience, they would say: "We, too, would like to reduce the deficit." But first they would like to crank it way up to get everybody on side. This government was mean-spirited, this government did not give enough to the seniors, this government did not give enough for education.

Hear, hear!

There they go! I've got them clapping already, Mr. Speaker, because they want more. But then they have not decided in fact how they are going to pay for more.
My colleague in the Liberal party is starting to laugh because he sees the folly of the thinking over there. Yes, Felix, yes, Mr. Member of Parliament from Portage la Prairie, we do want more. Once again you fell into your own trap. That is why you do not get elected as a government because people are so afraid of the irresponsible actions and positions that you bring forward in the House of Commons.
In fact, maybe you belong in that corner from now till eternity to represent some of those radical left-wing views. Certainly, some constituents will say: "I have a good representative in Ottawa. He is a marvellous chap, or a wonderful lady. He really represents the way I would like to spend money. They sit sanctimoniously and righteously and say that what we are doing is wrong. Yet if they were ever in power we would probably have to borrow twice this amount. Not $25 billion. That would be peanuts for those people over there. They would have to borrow $50 billion, maybe $100 billion.
They know how to spend. But you will not find an individual in that party who knows how to balance a business sheet and knows how to make economies tick because they come from a background of non-business. They come from some sort of a social welfare background. They do not know that this country is built on hard work, people who work hard and contribute.
By the way, the Tory Parliament is represented by a cross-section of Canadians. I mean, you have them right down from pig farmers like myself to doctors, lawyers, accountants, business people, and truck drivers. I would like to take a look at the cross-section of that particular group over there in the corner because I am sure it is not veiy different. One almost has the same profession as the next, to spend money.

Mr. Speaker, the borrowing authority is traditionally an occasion in the House of Commons when members are able to debate economic policy of the government, and it is my regret that on this occasion the government has chosen to cut off debate before that discussion has taken place. There is certainly much to be said about the government's failure to provide real economic leadership in our economy, real economic leadership to the Canadian people.

March 29, 1990
Government Orders
It is a well known tenet of basic economics that a short-term deficit can be a major way of promoting growth and demand during a downturn in a business cycle. The opposite side of that equation is that when the economy re-enters a period of growth, public expenditure must be reined in, both to reduce inflationaiy pressures in the economy and to repay the debt which the government incurred when it was stimulating the economy.
This government has shown no evidence of real commitment to constraint in its spending during the past eight years of remarkable prosperity; prosperity I might point out which was to a substantial degree triggered and augmented by the spending of the previous government during a period of economic recession.
The single failure of this government to employ both fiscal and monetary policy to restore our economy to growth and expansion is everywhere evident. Since the 1981 recession, Canada has experienced uninterrupted economic growth. Yet during this period the government has allowed the public debt to more than double. The public debt is well over twice today what it was when this government entered office.
In 1988, for example, the net financial debt of the federal government, the provincial governments and the local governments across Canada was about $400 billion or over $15,000 for every Canadian. Among the other major members of the OECD, only Britain and Italy had a higher debt to gross national product ratio.
The growth of this debt is of even more concern than its size. Admittedly, there has been some modest progress in reducing the ratio of expenditures to revenue. In 1984, when the deficit reached its peak, federal expenditures were equal to 24 per cent of GDP, whereas federal revenues were only 17 per cent. By 1988, the government reminds us, federal expenditures had dropped to 21 per cent of GDP and revenues through tax increases had risen to over 18 per cent. These modest gains were more than offset by the dramatic rise in interest rates and accordingly in debt service charges.
According to the finance minister's last budget, average interest rates for the next year are forecast at over 11 per cent, while Canada's growth rate will average no more than 2 per cent.
When interest rates are higher than the rate of growth, the stage obviously is set for a further explosion in the public debt. Under these circumstances, the primary budget, that is excluding net interest payments, must generate a surplus sufficient to offset the growth in interest costs, if an increase in the debt is to be avoided. In other words, increases in revenue and reductions in government expenditure are both needed simply to overcome the rising costs of the public debt. Yet there is no evidence that interest rates will fall dramatically in the short-term, despite the Finance Minister's optimistic predictions.
Largely as a result of six years of government overspending, inflation is now running at more than 5 per cent. Moreover, escalating rates in Japan and in western Europe will force the Bank of Canada, if it chooses to continue its present policies, to raise its own interest rates if Canada wants to continue to attract foreign capital and to maintain international confidence in our dollar.
This afternoon, I think we will see interest rates increase yet again. There is certainly every reason to believe that interest rates will be even higher than those forecast by the Minister of Finance not a month ago.
What are the implications for Canadians of this mismanagement of our economy? First, we increase our net foreign liabilities. Of course, many Canadian corporations, public utilities and provincial governments traditionally have borrowed abroad. Recently, however, the national government also has turned to offshore borrowing as a way of financing its debt and its expenditures. About 30 per cent of Canadian Government bonds are now held by foreigners. With the current high levels of interest, an increasing share of wealth will now be siphoned off abroad in order to pay those debts.
Moreover, the Canadian government will become that much more addicted to high interest rates and a high Canadian dollar, if it is to continue to attract the high levels of foreign capital it believes that it needs to finance its operations and its growing debt.
March 29, 1990

The second major implication for Canada is that private investment will be discouraged by the present fiscal and monetary policies of this government. The high levels of taxation needed to finance the federal deficit has undoubtedly served to crowd out domestic investment. The Canadian economy today needs about $100 billion a year to finance itself. But since only $40 billion of this can be supplied from consumer savings in Canada, the economy looks offshore for almost $60 billion a year.
Moreover, the government's failure to solve its debt problem has raised further concerns about future levels of taxation. That, in turn, undoubtedly discourages private sector capital formation.
Further, given the current differential between domestic and international interest rates, Canadian businesses are encouraged to draw upon foreign savings, and these foreign borrowings have in turn pushed exchange rates for the Canadian dollar far beyond what our productivity would seem to warrant. The implications of a high Canadian dollar for our existing and future trade opportunities, particularly in light of our increased vulnerability to the United States, is obvious.
I want to remind the House for one moment that when we speak of government borrowing, we are also speaking of a form of social inequity. We are redistributing wealth upwards from the less affluent sectors in our society. It is after all, every Canadian who ultimately pays interest on the public debt. And since this debt is held mainly by more affluent Canadians, it is clear that there is a negative redistribution of wealth from the bottom up.
There is much more to be said about the government's present fiscal and monetary policies, but since it has chosen to cut off debate, I shall have to satisfy myself with these few comments.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise today to speak to Bill C-65, a bill with which the government wishes to borrow $25.5 billion.
This borrowing is fundamental to our government's objectives as they were presented in the recent budget. Our objectives are to cut spending and reduce the deficit. I know that the people of Calgary North are very concerned about these objectives and want to see them
Government Orders
accomplished. Any delay in passing this bill will interfere with these objectives.
There is a growing understanding in my riding about the need not only to cut expenditures as we have, but to continue to cut expenditures in the future.
The people of my riding understand that when the government took office in 1984 spending was out of control. Over $25 billion a year was being spent in terms of the balance between revenue and operating costs of the government. At that time, the government was spending $16 billion more than it was receiving in revenues. At the present time, we are spending $9 billion less than we are receiving in revenues. Despite all this, we have heard many objections about some of the actions of the government, such as the plan to bring in the goods and services tax.
My constituents realize the need to reorganize the tax system. They realize that a fundamental part of our budget is to restructure the tax system so that we have a clear-cut, visible consumption tax as well as an income tax. These are two fundamental objectives that any government should have. Those who use in society should pay in proportion to their use, and those who gain from society should pay in proportion to that gain. These are the fundamental objectives of any tax system. We have undertaken to revise the manufacturers' sales tax which is such an insidious detriment to our economy.
In Alberta, we need to free up our industry. At the present time most people do not realize that the manufacturers' sales tax means that some 1 per cent to 2 per cent of the cost of production of oil and gas exported consists of manufacturers' sales tax. For the companies operating in Alberta this means that that 1 per cent extra revenue could mean as much as a 10 per cent increase in their profits. That profit would certainly go toward improving the economy of Alberta.
With regard to the GST, I think it is also important to note that senior citizens in our area are beginning to understand how important this move is to them and that they will not be hit detrimentally by this tax. Many of them are now waiting with some anticipation for the rebates of the GST which they will receive every three months.
I was also interested to receive a delegation from the Calgary Real Estate Board. I assumed they would be telling me they were against the GST because I had heard about many individual real estate agents in my riding telling customers to buy now because prices would go up when the GST came in. But the members of the Calgary Real Estate Board acknowledged to me that only about a 1 per cent increase would take place in

March 29, 1990
Government Orders
home prices for normal-sized homes-that is up to $350,000 in Calgary-and that in fact rate of increase that takes place normally in the market roughly every two weeks in Calgary, due to the vibrant economy that we have.
Bill C-65 is simply a borrowing bill that will allow the government to get on with its job, to reduce the deficit to some $28.5 billion this coming year, and to bring it into balance in 1995. This is a difficult and, slow process, but it is important to understand that the deficit that we now have is not primarily the result of the actions of this government. This government inherited a deficit of some $200 billion and, admittedly, while it was trying to crank the spending down, it spent another $30 billion or so in addition to the revenue that it was receiving. During that time, the interest alone has added some $150 billion of interest so that we now have a debt in the order of $380 billion.
The hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier indicated that we would not tell him or the House how this money that we want to borrow is going to be spent. Every detail of how we want to spend this money has been presented in the budget. The budget has outlined clearly such things as transfers to persons, some $35 billion. This $35 billion is not affected by the restraint program and the elderly will benefit to the tune of some $17.5 billion of that amount for the old age security program, the guaranteed income supplement and the spouses' allowance. The increase in this spending is due to the increased numbers of people receiving these benefits. But we have limited the increase by introducing a 15 per cent repayment program for those individuals whose net income is over $50,000. This further restrains the amount that we need to borrow under this bill.
Under the transfers to persons, the unemployed will receive some $13.3 billion. This is an increase in the amount of money spent on unemployment, despite the reduction in the level of unemployment in the country. The dollars are up because the benefits are up. We have also, quite rightly, introduced structural reform which will restrain the amount of money that we need to borrow under this bill.
Under the family allowances program, some $2.7 billion will be paid out. Admittedly, this is a lower amount than in previous years because we have fewer payments due to the smaller size of families. Again, we have been responsible in capping and restraining the need to borrow by introducing the 15 per cent repayment for those whose individual net income exceeds the $50,000.
Veterans payments remain unchanged at $1.3 billion.
There are other payments which are, of course, outlined in detail in the budget. There are the transfers to governments of $36.1 billion. These payments are being made to provincial, territorial and municipal governments, $24 billion in straight cash and $12.1 billion in tax transfers.
There is Established Programs Financing. The growth of this program has been reduced by 2 per cent in 1989 and 1 per cent more in 1990. This is further action taken by our government to cut spending and reduce the need to borrow.
The Progressive Conservative government has introduced programs to reduce spending in virtually every area and has kept the amount that we have to borrow under this bill to an absolute minimum.

Mr. Speaker, here we are again, instead of debating the contents of Bill C-65, an act to provide borrowing authority, debating another one of the government tactics to prevent debate, and that is closure. I do not know when the government is going to learn that when it brings important topics to the floor of the House, there should be no time allocation, there should be no closure.
Here is what a Canadian, the minister's friend from 401 Bay Street, Mr. Bruce Haines, thinks of the Prime Minister's and the minister's tactics of closure. I will quote from his letter:
Dear Prime Minister
You have resorted to closure in the House of Commons to fend off the avalanche of criticism directed against the GST and inundated newspapers with taxpayer-paid propaganda about the tax as if it was
March 29, 1990

already the law of the land. On the theory that a lie will gain acceptance if repeated often enough, you have urged Canadians to believe that the 7 percent GST is little more than a benign replacement of the 13-1/2 percent Federal Sales Thx (which was only 9 percent before you got elected and then only imposed on certain goods at the factory or manufacturing level).
Mr. Haines also says:
Never before have Canadians been treated so shabbily by a government which, against a nearly unanimous outcry, has expressed a determination to saddle them with the biggest and most cynical tax grab in history, the GST-Why should Canadians trust you with another dime?
On February 28, 1990, the Hon. Minister of Finance said that he was proud that he has moved, and I quote "further and faster" than his counterpart in the United Kingdom. I would suggest to him that he slow down, because if he does not, he is going to find himself out in the cold, way ahead of his hero in 1992. The race is on. Which of the two parties in question is going to be first in the loss of support among its own party colleagues? The standings to date show a draw, one Tory riding in Canada to one Tory riding in the United Kingdom. We are not even out of the starting gates.
In the United Kingdom, the last straw was the introduction of what is commonly referred to as the poll tax, a tax levied on the number of adults in a household. Estimates done by officials had put the average expected tax at approximately $565 Canadian a person. The actuals come in at approximately $742 Canadian, a difference of approximately $180 Canadian a person. This is not per household but per person. That means that for a family of four, it will cost $800 Canadian more in a year in taxes than anticipated. That is no joke.
This example begs the question of exactly how accurate the estimates that are being thrown around by our hon. minister are with respect to the GST. It also begs the question as to what exactly the government wants to achieve. Granted, the bottom line in the United Kingdom looks good in terms of financial management, but let us look at the underlying side effects of the numbers. In other words, let us look at the effects suffered by the people of the United Kingdom.
In the words of Andrew Gamble, a professor of politics at the University of Sheffield, and I quote:
-the policies of Mrs. Thatcher precipitated a major shake-out of labour and the destruction of a large part of Britain's manufacturing capacity pushing millions into poverty, destroying and demoralizing
Government Orders
many communities and accelerating the decay of the inner cities and the older manufacturing areas.
According to the OECD statistics, in every year of this decade unemployment has been higher in the U.K. than any other of the summit seven leading industrialized countries. In the latest comparable statistics from OECD, unemployment in the U.K. was over 50 per cent higher than the average of the other countries.
This will sound familiar to most of my colleagues in the House but this was as a result of cut-backs in public spending and borrowing, direct tax cuts that were counterbalanced by indirect taxes, increases via the infamous VAT which caused the burden of taxes to rise.
There are approximately three million unemployed in the United Kingdom. Beggars defined as less deserving, not less fortunate, have become a tragic visible symbol of the country's policies.
If these are the types of policies admired and embraced by the government, we are in big trouble. We better start to defeat this government now because in a few years this country will bear no resemblance to what we have come to know as Canada.
We will be in the same situation as the United Kingdom. Thank you very much but, personally, I do not want to see more food banks as a result of more families starving. I do not want to see more people sleeping on the streets than are already there. God knows I have enough of those in my riding. I have absolutely no interest in seeing one of my country's most valuable and essential resources such as water being privatized.
The hon. minister has been tightening the belts of Canadians for six years, "for their own good" he says. If the government can rid itself of the deficit all Canadians will benefit from it. Yet, he insists on keeping interest rates high-and I expect they will go even higher today-forcing the debt to grow even larger at the same time and increasing taxes and cutting back on programs for the most needy Canadians.
It reminds me of a story of a hotel owner in the Klondike who fired his bartender. "Why?", he was asked. "Because he was crooked," was the answer. "I watered the whiskey and watered the whiskey and I still couldn't make any money." The minister has been watering services to the public. He has been watering his

Government Orders
commitment to the public. He has been watering down the pockets of Canadians.
All over the world, people are opening up to new ideas. Here we have a rehashing of ideas that did not work in 1985, 1986, 1987, 1988 and 1989. But for some reason they are all of a sudden going to work in 1990. The Minister of Finance said: "We have to be more productive and more competitive." He continues to reduce budgets for R-D and science and technology. He has cut, not reduced, transfer payments to provinces that will result in an incredible rise in the cost of higher education.
Are we going to harmonize our educational system with that of the Americans? The average tuition of a state university-and I am not talking about Harvard. I am talking about an ordinary university-is $18,000 American a year. Are we going to be more competitive when Canadians can no longer afford to educate themselves? Education is the most important weapon against poverty. It is the most important tool for our younger generations in trying to secure for themselves an adequate standard of living.
This fact obviously escapes my hon. colleague, the minister, who plays politics with the future of our country by passing the buck. It begs the question, the quality of brainpower behind this fudge-it budget. The priorities of this government are based on money, not people. They do not reflect the spirit of Canada. If the Prime Minister could manage to limit himself to a pair of shoes, like the majority of Canadians are forced to do, maybe a homeless family could move into his closet.
I am not trying to be funny. The question of homeless people is a growing one as less Canadians are able to afford both food and shelter. Yet this government decides to cut the social housing budget by 15 per cent in 1990-91 and a further 15 per cent in 1991-92. Over five years this budget will lose $165 million. There are over
200,000	homeless people in Canada and a further 84,000 a month who, after paying rent, have a mere $23 a week to spend on food, medicine and clothes.
The number of people using emergency food programs in Metro Toronto has doubled over the past three years. The average income of people who are forced to use
food banks is higher than in 1987, but the remaining income after rent is not.
According to a special report by the Daily Bread Food Bank located in my riding, a food bank agency that is very credible around the world-and I want to give them credit and congratulate them-states that this fact implies that people with higher incomes who were not food bank users in 1987 can no longer make ends meet today because rental costs leave them with insufficient funds to buy basic necessities. This government is picking on the very Canadians who need help the most. They have cut funding to groups for the poor, disabled persons, women, minorities, natives and seniors. To add insult to injury, we are told that we do not understand the issue. We are told that we do not understand why the government has to cut back. We are told that if we really understand the GST, we would welcome the tax. This government undermines the intelligence of Canadian people. Canadians will not accept the GST.
Mr. Speaker, I jut have one more sentence.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I regret the hon. member's time has expired. The hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak at a time when there is a cloud over this whole institution of Parliament. It is a cloud placed there by this government. After only three hours of debate on a bill to borrow some $25.5 billion, this government has again-I think it is the thirty-fifth time-invoked closure or time allocation.
Personally, I am annoyed because the last time the GST was debated in the House I was unable to speak because of closure. I was too far down the list and time ran out.
Most people in my riding are very upset with the way the government is muzzling members of this House. They are also upset with the way the government is running this country with respect to taxes. They are upset when the minister says there are no new tax increases in the budget and that is not true. They are upset when the minister says that we went through good times but now it is time to tighten our belts. People in the Moose Jaw-Lake Centre riding, who are they? They are mainly seniors, small business people, farmers and workers. They are middle income earners and lower
March 29, 1990

middle income earners. They do not mind paying their fair share of taxes, but that is not what is happening.
In Saskatchewan services and opportunities are drying up. In Moose Jaw businesses are closing at an alarming rate and housing prices are depressed. Saskatchewan alone in the last four years has lost some 50,000 people. That is 50,000 people out of a population of one million. We have 14 per cent of our population living below the poverty line. This is the second highest in the country. We have no Conrad Blacks or others of his ilk. We have no major corporations that made some $27 billion in profits and pay no income tax. We do not have those types of people. For the minister to tell the people in Moose Jaw-Lake Centre that they have to tighten their belts is simply insulting and they realize how much this government has lost touch with the people of this country.
This government is good at misleading Canadians. The finance minister says there are no tax increases in the budget. That is not true. The GST is certainly a budget bill and will increase taxes in the country to bring in an extra $5 billion in revenue a year. There is another item that the government has conveniently overlooked as well. This year's budget is really a continuation of last year's budget where cuts were made.
Because of the time, I will only focus on the area of agriculture which is important to Saskatchewan. In last year's budget announced over a year ago there were cuts that will take effect this year. Crop insurance, $110 million; at and east freight rates, $40 million; branch line rehabilitation, $4 million; advanced payments $27 million; dairy export program, $7 million; commodity-based loans, $8.5 million; Canadian Dairy Commission, $7 million; fuel tax rebate, $125 million. That is a total of $328.5 billion taken out of the agricultural economy this year from last year's budget. There are cuts and this year's budget is simply a continuation of last year's budget, pure and simple.
I have been speaking with many people in my riding who are upset and angry with this government. I would like to highlight one particular example. Mr. Bert Mick-leborough came into my office some time ago. Ele was outraged at the way the government is performing. Mr. Mickleborough has brought in tax receipts and pay stubs
Government Orders
for me to bring to the House today. He has indicated that he voted for the Progressive Conservatives in the past but certainly will not do so in the future.
I would like to outline Mr. Mickleborough's situation which is not untypical of the riding. Mr. Mickleborough is 35 years of age and lives in Moose Jaw. He is married and has two children aged 11 and 8. He is a certified engineer technician. He is working and not living off the government. He is not taking the dole. He has never been on unemployment insurance. He is a hard working member of the community.
Mr. Mickleborough feels outraged when the Minister of Finance says that Canadians have been living beyond their means. He has not. He is maintaining a very small debt, lives in a 1,100 square foot bi-level with three bedrooms, does not take holidays to Disneyland but may drive to Medicine Hat, 200 miles down the road for a holiday. He is not living beyond his means. He is outraged at this suggestion. He is so upset that he gave me his receipts indicating that in 1983 on a two-week basis his cheques were $1,320. They are now $1,722.40 which is a 30 per cent increase. However, his tax has gone up from $365.08 to $506.34 which is a 39 per cent increase.
Mr. Mickleborough is a middle income Canadian earning approximately $40,000 a year whose taxes have increased faster than his income. Now he has to face the GST tax. This typical Canadian did not intend to rock any boats. He is happy, but is so upset by statements of this government that he has come forward to ask me to bring these facts to the attention of the House.
What we need is a government which will bring forth a budget that will build for tomorrow, that has a strong commitment to the environment, that has a plan to build and sustain regional economies, that will cut the interest rate to support economic growth and restore and improve social programs. We need a government that will allow families such as the Mickleborough family to live and work in an environment that will encourage them to do that type of work.
We have lots of Mickleboroughs across the country who are hard working Canadians, who deserve better than this and are being simply ignored by this government.

March 29, 1990
Mr. Speaker, I realize my time is just about up. I would like to conclude by saying that we do need a government that will listen to all Canadians and not just to the upper crust such as the Conrad Blacks. We need a government that will respect the needs of Canadians and to allow them to have healthy, happy and productive families. This government failed to do that in the past. It continues to fail to do that now.
Bert Mickleborough is typical of many voters throughout this country and he certainly intends to let the government know his feelings next time when it really counts at the next federal general election.

Mr. Speaker, there is great concern among the snow crab fishermen of Prince Edward Island that their livelihoods will be endangered if the Department of Fisheries and Oceans drastically reduces the snow crab quota in P.E.I. zones.
It is my opinion that Prince Edward Island should not have a restricted zone. P.E.I. snow crab fishermen should have open access to the fishery, equal to the access that the New Brunswick and Quebec fishermen have.
It is discriminatory that my fishermen have to stay within a small zone which is open to the other Atlantic Canada fishermen. Prince Edward Island's 30 licenced permit holders must have a quota which both sustains their incomes and keeps the high quality crab processing line operating at the Tignish Fisheries Co-op.
Our crab fishermen support the concept of a management plan for the fishery. Stocks have been depleted and the remaining stock must be managed for the long-term benefit of all concerned.
Prince Edward Island crab fishermen were the first to exploit and develop the snow crab fishery in Atlantic Canada. I urge the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans to deal fairly with this matter. That is all we expect and ask for fair and equal treatment. Five per cent of total catch based on landings of the past five years would meet the minimum requirements of P.E.I.'s crab fishermen.

Mr. Speaker, many members of Parliament received visits by the Jewish Students Network this week. These very concerned and thoughtful young people are getting us thinking about some very basic questions. Why is Soviet President Gorbachev opening the gates to freedom of expression and glasnost but not letting Jewish people out of Russia? Why is anti-Semitism growing in the Soviet Union? Why are so many Jewish refusnik cases still outstanding? In short, why is there developing a very ugly persecution of the Jewish people in the Soviet Union?
I want to commend the leadership of the Jewish Students Network on their initiative in creating freedom for millions of Soviet Jews. I also want to urge the Canadian government to continue to press Moscow to open any gates possible to the 30,000 exit visas for Soviet Jews which are still outstanding.
President Gorbachev, please tear down your own wall against the Jewish people.

Mr. Speaker, agriculture is a key part of the Canadian economy. Farming and related industries provide one job in ten, and the agri-food sector must not be neglected, since it accounts for 10 per cent of the gross national product.
However, it is important to remember that agricultural productivity depends on the condition of the soil, and the week of April 9 to 15 again this year will be devoted to making Canadians aware of this resource that we must protect.
March 29, 1990

Mr. Speaker, the Conservative government has understood the critical importance of agriculture to us and therefore last year it instituted a three-year national soil conservation program.
