speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, according to the federal government's own figures, we are still not replanting every hectare of forest land we harvest. In 1987, the last year for which figures are available, there was a shortfall of
200,000	unplanted hectares. Despite this, this government has failed to renew forest agreements with Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario.
The current agreement with British Columbia expires on Saturday and the minister said he likely will not be able to sign a new one. He has even called the provinces' plans to clean up our backlog of harvested areas unreasonable. What is unreasonable is the complete failure of the Ministers of Forestry and the Environment to use effectively the programs currently available to regenerate and manage our forests.
The minister should sign those agreements today so that we can ensure that our forests are replanted and the necessary research is done to sustain our forests for the future.

Mr. Speaker, last Saturday, March 24, 1990,1 had the distinct honour to join with many leaders of the Ismaili Muslim Community in a ground breaking ceremony in Markham for the Ismaili Torrent North Central Jamatkhana which will be built over this year.
The Ismaili Muslim leaders at this historic ceremony included Nizar Kanji, the Canadian president for His Highness Prince Aga Khan Council; Mohamad Manji, the Ontario president for His Highness Prince Aga Khan
Council and His Excellency Tariq Altaf, consul general of Pakistan.
Also at this special ceremony was Barkat Ali, an Ismaili Muslim leader from Markham who first approached the mayor of Markham to obtain a piece of land for the construction of the Jamatkhana.
This special occasion marked yet another milestone in the establishment of strong institutions across Canada by the Ismaili Community and reflects their tolerance, generosity, industry and spirit of voluntarism for all Canadians.
This initiative also speaks of the Ismaili Muslim community's gratitude to His Highness Prince Aga Khan who has 20 million followers around the world.

Mr. Speaker, a direct, non-stop air service between the national capital region and Chicago is vital if the economy of the capital region is to continue to diversify, reducing its dependence on federal government employment and contributing to Canada's competitiveness in the world economy.
The community of Ottawa-Hull is the fourth largest urban Canadian centre. It is not reasonable that the competitiveness of this region is hampered because business trips that could be accomplished in two and a half hours now take seven to eight hours. Business that could be done in a day now takes two days, resulting in extra costs and the loss of productivity.
It is inconceivable that international travellers are unable to access the capital of Canada conveniently, economically and efficiently.
I challenge the Government of Canada to do its part in agreeing to Ottawa-Hull as a co-terminus with Montreal on the Montreal-Chicago route.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today in an attempt to educate the hon. Minister of National Defence.

March 29, 1990
I would like to read a passage from a recent mailing to the Minister's Saskatchewan constituency in which the Minister said: "Saskatchewan does not have any defence establishments."
This will come as quite a surprise to the 1,300 personnel at Canadian Forces Base Moose Jaw which, the last time I checked, was still in Saskatchewan, still one of the busiest airports in North America and still home of the internationally acclaimed Snowbirds.
This will also come as quite a shock to my constituents in the city of Moose Jaw who benefit from the $55 million that the base contributes annually to the local economy.
Given the experience of Summerside, P.E.I. and Portage la Prairie, Manitoba, the question must be asked: Was the minister simply exhibiting ignorance of his ministry and his home province of Saskatchewan, or was he committing the proverbial Freudian slip?

Mr. Speaker, I want to bring to the government's attention, a very serious situation for Canadian companies resulting from the Canada-U.S. Trade Agreement.
Some of you will know that under the Accelerated Elimination of Tariffs Agreement, products classified under Tariff No. 4201 will have tariffs removed on April 1.
One product group in this classification has successfully appealed, but others now have little time. They just found out recently that time was running out.
Unless action is taken now, companies such as Western Rawhide and Harness Manufacturing Company will have to lay-off their remaining production staff long before the expected date of 1995 or 1996. In fact, perhaps they will have to do it immediately.
The company will end up being a distributor of American made products. I call on the government to act now. This is but one example out of the many which are going to be affected in Canada.

The company is counting on the government. The employees and their families are counting on the government.

Mr. Speaker, in the course of my reading the other day, I came across an editorial on the dual language debate, a part of which I would like to read into the record in this House:
It behooves the people of this Canada of ours, French and English, to stand shoulder to shoulder, forgetting the differences of opinion which may exist between us and only remembering the great love we bear for our country, to push forward in the great work of building up a nationality in Canada which shall be able to challenge the applause and admiration of the world. Then the time will have come in the history of Canada when the proudest words a citizen of this country can utter will be, "I am a Canadian."
The interesting part of this editorial is that it was written on March 6, 1890.
It is repeated by me in March of 1990 and I want us to resolve that no one will be making statements like that in March of 2090. Let us, from this day forward, make our language duality a source of unity and not divisiveness in this country.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the previous statement.
Yesterday I received two letters from constituents in Delta, and I would like to quote briefly from them.
The first, one said: "Let me say I hope Quebec stays with us. They are a great people". The writer then goes on to tell of his very positive experience in World War II with his Quebec compatriots.
The second letter says: "With regard to the present turmoil surrounding the Meech Lake Accord, I would like to see more feeling put into making our Canadian French feel more at home in this country". Then the
March 29, 1990

writer goes on to give some practical ways in which this might be done.
This is a very critical time in Canada's history, as these Delta residents have shown. It is a time for understanding, patience, goodwill and effective dialogue. Canada without Quebec is unthinkable. It is time for all Canadians, east and west, north and south, to preserve this magnificent country that has such a vital role to play in the future of our whole planet, let alone ourselves and our children.

Mr. Speaker, the just released discussion paper for the Environmental Action Plan shows that this government has let Canadians down with its lack of concrete action to tackle environmental problems.
But this Green Plan serves only to buy the government time, while the Minister of the Environment struggles to convince his Cabinet colleagues of the necessity and the virtue of strong programs. Meanwhile, over 900 chemicals in the Great Lakes still have no federal standards. We are the world's largest producer of garbage, the greatest consumer of energy, one of the leading emitters of carbon dioxide, and the Tories fumble with a Federal Court order on the Oldman River Dam.
This Green Plan is just the latest example of Tory policy: All talk, no action. Canadians want concrete action taken on the environment, with measurable goals in a specific time frame with national standards.

Mr. Speaker, by cutting $4.1 million from heritage language programs, the government is turning its back on multiculturalism. Many of the 1,500 classes across Canada will be forced to close.
Heritage language classes cost very little, but their cultural and economic value is great. They promote cultural identity and family unity. While the Minister for
International Trade spends $14 million on Pacific Rim languages, children are denied language classes.
Leaders of major ethnic groups in Ottawa today demand continued funding. The government must listen to one-third of Canadians whose origin is neither French nor English, who demand their rights as taxpayers to funding for their children to learn their mother tongue.
CEC says cuts are bad for Canadian culture, bad for education, bad for international trade and bad for national unity.
I call on the Minister of State for Multiculturalism and Citizenship to fulfil his multicultural responsibility by reinstating full funding for heritage languages immediately.

Mr. Speaker, the women occupying the Secretary of State offices in St. John's, Newfoundland have now spent four frustrating days calling for the reinstatement of funding to the women's program.
Last night, the Secretary of State graciously allowed some of his senior officials to meet with the protesters. Unfortunately, the only message they were allowed to bring was that they had no authority to reinstate the $1.6 million cut from last month's budget.
Even the senior Newfoundland cabinet minister himself, the Minister for International Trade, pointed out to the Secretary of State that the main issue is not money, but a drastic change in Secretary of State policy. Is this change in policy an attempt to stifle the voice of Canadian women?
Two ministers have now made representation to the Secretary of State to restore these funds. Does Cabinet speak with one voice, or with a forked tongue? Canadian women and men demand that the Secretary of State reinstate funding immediately. At the very least, he must meet with the St. John's Status of Women group, face to face and stop sending powerless bureaucrats.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to commend and encourage the people of Lithuania.

March 29, 1990
Oral Questions
We must never forget the recent history when, from 1939 to 1941, they were forcibly annexed to the Soviet Union. Recently, however, we have witnessed the rebirth of this small country.
I am sure all members of this House would want to say: "We are one with you in your historic struggle for democracy and your right of self-determination. We encourage you and we admire your bravery".

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. For more than a year, the government has been talking about the environment and has made all kinds of promises. Mr. Speaker, to answer my honorable friend, quite a bit has been achieved in this area. I am thinking of international agreements concluded by this government. For instance, we were the first country at the Vienna Convention to ratify an agreement on protecting the ozone layer, and we concluded an agreement with the Soviet Union on November 1989. Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
Today, the Canadian bank rate rose more than 13 basis points to 13.51 per cent. That is the highest level since the Prime Minister and his government were sworn in in September of 1984.

Mr. Speaker, the very simple answer is that we want to avoid the problems of 1980 and 1982, when we saw interest rates under the government that he supported at 20 per cent to 25 per cent. That was a lesson-a very, very tough one-for everybody across this country. It is a lesson from which we must learn. It is a lesson that we do not want to see repeated.
It means that we must get inflation under control. That requires us to continue doing the things that we are doing, whether it is through monetary policy or through budgetary policy, to ensure that we get the level of inflation under control and not sweep it under the carpet as his government did. We must face it head on. That is the way we will get lower interest rates. That is the way we will get lower interest rates on a much more permanent basis. Mr. Speaker, I would like to put the usual Thursday afternoon question to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons and ask him about his plans for the business of the House. Second, I have a very important question I would like the government to answer, and I see the Prime Minister is in the House. I would be grateful for his attention.
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, but it also concerns the Prime Minister. We have not had a deputy speaker of the House for nearly a month and I would like to ask the government what it intends to do about filling this position and what the procedure will be. Will there be an election at large, as is the case for the Speaker or are there other procedures? Why the delay? Why don't we have a deputy speaker?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tomorrow will be an opposition day. Monday will be the last day of debate on second reading of Bill C-65, the borrowing authority bill. Tuesday we start the report stage of Bill C-62, the GST bill. As for the rest of the week, we shall see.

In terms of the question respecting the Deputy Speaker, it will be happening very soon and it will be done in the way prescribed in the McGrath commission report. As we know, the recommendation was that the position of Speaker be elected and the other positions be appointed in the traditional manner. That will happen and happen very soon.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Standing Orders also say "forthwith". That means immediately. We have been very patient with the government. They know that, and I think they will recognize that we have accepted once in the absence of Mr. Speaker that the replacement for the Speaker not be the Deputy Speaker. That was a concession the opposition made.
We will not continue to wait until the government makes up its mind as to how we are going to cope with

March 29, 1990
Speaker's Ruling
that problem. It may be a difficult solution to a difficult problem. Why is the government not giving us a solution to the problem? Just put someone up for election and then we will proceed as we usually do.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that will happen forthwith. I am not sure why the hon. member is so exercised. If someone should be exercised perhaps the present occupants of the chair should be, bearing in mind their numbers, and we appreciate that.
The House leader of the Liberal Party will recognize that there is no Machiavellian scheme afoot to try to make life miserable for the opposition or any other such thing. There is in fact a busy schedule and very soon the concerns of the hon. member will be met.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps I could say to the hon. House leader that the sooner the better.

Mr. Speaker, on the subject of House business, I should also like to ask the government House leader about Bill C-61, an amendment to the Divorce Act, which was of great interest to the former Minister of Justice and is of great interest to me as well.
The legislation has now been through committee and it has been reported. I wonder if the minister might be prepared to call it at an early date.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Indeed I have a considerable list of important legislation including that, which I am most anxious to get before the House and completed and in place. I hope he will make representations to his colleagues, the House leader and the deputy House leader of the Liberal Party, as well as the New Democrats, so we might reach some agreement between us on how to proceed in an expeditious and effective fashion.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
I just heard the Minister of Transport saying: "I thought you were the House leader for the Liberals". I am, Mr. Speaker. I want to remind the former House leader that in those days at least we knew where we were going. Now we do not.
We were told this week that Bill C-26 would be called on Friday. Now we learn at 3.05 p.m. that it is not going to be Bill C-26; it is going to be an opposition day. We cannot operate this House in that manner. Either this House leader gets his act together and tells us what the agenda is for the next week, or he tells us every day what the business of the House will be the next day. That way we might at least have some knowledge of what we are
going to be looking at. I find it difficult to have a negotiating period on Tuesdays and have it changed on Thursdays.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a great deal of sympathy for that. I realize that when people make plans for Fridays, as we did last week, and have those changed at the last minute-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: That was not my fault; that was your own doing.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member is correct in saying that it was not his fault. This is not some sort of get even situation. It is simply a case of being unable to get assurances that in fact we would be able to proceed expeditiously with that bill. Had we had those assurances, we could do it, but without those assurances we are in a situation of again having to ask people to break their plans, to cancel engagements, to come back and so on to be here in order not to be bush-whacked, as it were, by dilatory motions and so on.
I regret that we have to do it that way. I again say that it is not my preference. I would much rather we sat down and negotiated a situation, and people kept to their word. We have not been able to reach that stage. I am willing to continue to try and I think the hon. member is. Between the two of us, maybe we can convince the third party to co-operate, and we could all serve our country a lot more effectively.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF AT AND EAST PROGRAM-SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
On February 12, 1990, the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre rose claiming that a contempt of Parliament may have been committed. The hon. member explained that in its budget of April 27, 1989 the government announced the elimination of the "at and east" grain and flour subsidy program, effective July 15, 1989.
The cancellation of this program took place prior to the adoption of any legislation by Parliament, which would have repealed Section 281 of the Railway Act, the statute which first established this program.
This action, the hon. member contends, is a contempt of Parliament and impedes the House from giving proper consideration to the bill presently before it at second
March 29, 1990

reading, since the proposed objective of the bill is already a fait accompli.

The next day, the Chair heard further argument on this point and wishes to thank the hon. members for Kingston and the Islands, Regina-Lumsden and Peace River who made perceptive and eloquent interventions. The Chair reserved on the matter and stated it would come back at a later date to render its decision. The Chair is now prepared to deliver that decision.

Basically the issue which the Chair must decide is whether or not the government has committed a contempt of Parliament by eliminating the "at and east" program, prior to the adoption of Bill C-26, an act to amend the Railway Act (grain and flour subsidies). The proposed legislation seeks to amend section 281 of the Railway Act, which would allow the railways to charge commercial rates, effective July 16, 1989.
The removal of the "at and east" program was part of the budget measures announced by the government on April 27, 1989. As all hon. members realize, budgets do not deal only with the raising of revenues. They also enunciate the fiscal, economic and even social policies of the government. The hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre did make a distinction between retroactive tax legislation emanating from a budget and legislation proposing to end a specific program.
With regard to the "at and east" program, the general practices of the House relating to budgets appear to have been applied. An announcement was included in the budget statement, the government made it effective shortly thereafter, and enabling legislation, namely Bill C-26, was introduced. Bill C-26 was read a first time on June 16,1989 and has been debated at second reading on February 12 and on February 20, 1990.
The essence of the matter raised by the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre is that the government announced May 4, 1989: "That the 'at and east' program
Speaker's Ruling
would be eliminated effective July 15, 1989," and that today, some eight months later, Parliament has not yet passed the legislation to this effect.

In his presentation, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands recalled at some length similar interventions made in 1971 by then-members of the opposition who were vigorously protesting the withholding of wheat payments in anticipation of the repeal of the Temporary Reserves Act which provided for such payments. The hon. member for Regina-Lumsden reminded the House of the eventual legal outcome of that 1971 situation in the Federal Court of Canada.

The Chair has been struck by the parallels between the 1971 wheat payment controversy and the situation before us relating to the "at and east" program. Indeed Speaker Lamoureux's decision is as illuminating today as it was then, for then as now the issue of whether the government is in violation of the law is not a question for the Chair to decide.
As Speaker Lamoureux explained on September 13, 1971, at page 7740 of Hansard'.
Whether the government has an obligation under the terms of the existing law to make certain payments is not a question for the Chair to decide.
The crux of the whole matter, as I understand it, is that the government is withholding payments authorized by an existing statute until a new statute has been adopted. Either what the government is doing is or is not contemplated, or anticipated, or authorized by the existing statute. Its action may well be subject to censure, but that would be a decision for the House to take.
Whether it is in order to use this method to induce the adoption of alternative government legislation can again be the subject of debate, but I suggest that this should not be done within the framework of the debate on a question of privilege.
In assessing the case before us today, the Chair must be solely concerned with the issue of whether or not the action of the government constitutes a contempt of Parliament by impeding the House from properly considering Bill C-26. A careful review of the situation leads me to conclude that the termination of the program was an administrative decision made by the executive.

March 29, 1990
Government Orders
The legality of such a decision is another question, but the decision of the government as such does not in any way impede the House from considering Bill C-26.

Nevertheless, that is not to say that this is a simple matter. The hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre has raised an issue of continuing concern: namely the implications of the practice whereby an initiative is implemented or a program terminated prior to the passage by Parliament of enabling legislation.

There can be little doubt that in having recourse to this approach a government must be ever mindful that Parliament makes the ultimate decision on the legislation before it. I have noted in the correspondence provided to me by the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre that the Ministry of Transport has been careful to advise the railway companies of the consequences if Parliament chooses not to approve this legislation and stresses the fact that it is still before the House.
The Chair agrees with the ruling of Speaker Lamou-reux in 1971 and therefore finds that this case does not fall within the ambit of privilege or contempt. The hon. member may well have a founded grievance in law, which he may wish to pursue in another place.
I commend the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre for drawing this important issue to the attention of the Chair and of the House. I also want to compliment him on the succinct and careful argument that he presented. I thank all other hon. members who participated in the decision for their contributions.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1990-91 ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-65
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before the House today, Bill C-65, would authorize the Conservative government to borrow $25 billion. That is 25 thousand million we are being asked to put in the hands of some totally irresponsible people. Since the last election in 1988, this government has acted totally irresponsibly, first of all on the subject of unemployment insurance; second, on VIA Rail; third, on the GST they are getting ready to impose on Canadians. Those are some of the reasons why we in the Liberal Party cannot afford to let this government go to the financial markets for $25 billion.
March 29, 1990

I truly deplore the attitude of this government which seems to be running our country on an ad hoc basis. They have completely lost control of public spending, Mr. Speaker. They are cutting right, left and centre, and they are totally oblivious to the impact of these cuts. They want to introduce new taxes without prior agreement with the provinces. They want to impose a new tax across Canada while ignoring our information on the market, inflation, and the new costs this will entail for Canadian citizens. Mr. Speaker, when a government has only 17 per cent of public support, it should be more anxious to consult, especially with the official opposition and in fact with the whole opposition.
Mr. Speaker, the government will very shortly impose closure on this bill as it has been doing recently on a number of bills. The government seems to want to muzzle the opposition because it no longer knows what it is doing.
Mr. Speaker, let me give you a few examples. Near the National Capital region, in my riding, on the other side of the Ottawa River, only a year ago Northern Telecom was closed. This, of course, was blamed on free trade.
Just recently, we learned that Catelli would continue operations in Montreal provided employees accepted large wage cuts. Otherwise, it would shut down and go to the United States. Nearer here, Les Placages de I'Ou-taouais just signed a new collective agreement yesterday or the day before allowing the company to hire nonunionized workers for $6 an hour to replace employees who used to earn $10 an hour. They said in fact, "Take it or we close down!" Mr. Speaker, is that what the Prime Minister means when he tells us that 200,000 jobs were created last year, while in the National Capital Region and especially in our area, they boast about cutting the Public Service by 15 per cent over the last four years, they almost boast about closing down businesses-
I just spoke about Northern Telecom. I could tell you about Les Boiseries de I'Outaouais; the Federal Business Development Bank refused to lend it money to keep it going. We could talk about the Museum of Civilization for which the government, through the National Capital Commission, last year, just a few months ago, announced
Government Orders
major cuts. That project, including the fountains costing $500,000, has still not been finished.
We remember all the patronage surrounding the construction of the Museum of Civilization, which originally was to cost $80 million and is now up to $260 million. That is where we should look, instead of imposing new taxes, continually sticking it to Canadians and making them bear the burden of mismanagement. That is where we should look!
The other day, I was examining the famous case of Transport Canada, and I want to look into it more closely soon. Last year the federal government decided to renew the lease at Place de Ville owned by Campeau Corporation. We know it will have to pay to remove the asbestos inside this building. The costs are estimated at some $100 million. A few weeks ago I was told that, should the government stay in its current location in Place de Ville where it faces major expenditures, after 20 years it will have paid over $900 million more than if it had awarded the contract last year to the lowest bidder who happened to be from the Outaouais. This is another example of mismanagement by this government that operates from day to day.
There were recent reports on CKCH, a local radio station, and in Le Droit that Canada Post was about to make major cuts in the Outaouais side of the National Capital Region and to eliminate sorting jobs in Hull, Aylmer and Gatineau. Cutting jobs left and right will not lead to economic recovery.
We, in the Liberal opposition, have given the government suggestions we consider realistic. There is a 5 per cent gap between the current interest rates set by the Bank of Canada and the American rates. How can Canadian businesses be competitive when our interest rates are so high and when the consumer always ends up paying for the damage?
Mr. Speaker, I believe the Opposition has presented you and the Government with solutions to try and reduce the current economic trend that is leading inevitably to a recession.
The government today is asking for authority to borrow $ 25 billion, which is 25 thousand million, Mr. Speaker! In order to do what? To go on managing on a daily basis as they are now doing, by restricting debate

March 29, 1990
Government Orders
because it is quite possible that in a few moments we will be denied the opportunity to further discuss the matter.
Well, Mr. Speaker, that will not work. The Liberal Opposition no longer can help or let this government rush us along the road to recession and increased inflation with the coming imposition of the For all those reasons and more, Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Opposition will flatly refuse to endorse any measure this government intends to force upon the Canadian people.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, and I insist on this because according to recent polls-and as we know public opinion polls, in Canada are accurate to a few percentage points-hardly 17 per cent of the Canadian people now approve of this government. Mr. Speaker, I believe this government is routed. This government whom the people no longer trust to lead them is preparing once more to introduce new taxes under the pretext of reducing the debt, reducing the deficit.
Mr. Speaker, I believe the Canadian people just as the Official Opposition no longer believe in this government's actions, and we cannot support Bill C-65 which would grant this government authority to borrow $ 25 billion.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1990-91 ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-65
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that I am debating the time allocation motion rather than Bill C-65 itself. The object of this time allocation motion is to limit debate on a bill that authorizes the government to borrow $25.5 billion on the credit of the people of Canada at interest rates that as of today have increased substantially.
My concern is that this government is acting in a more and more authoritarian manner and is dealing with this House of Commons in a more and more rigorous and dictatorial manner by ramming each and every piece of legislation through this House. As our House leader pointed out this morning, in the last 11 months this government has used closure or time allocation 15 times, more than any previous time in history. Since its term in office in the last six years it has used closure 30 times.
This government is abusing the House of Commons and abusing the rights and privileges of the members of the House of Commons by denying them the right to debate, in particular, the most important legislation
coming into this House. This piece of legislation is extremely important.
The government is asking the opposition to give it carte blanche to borrow something like $25.5 billion on the credit of the people of Canada. That simply cannot be done after a mere four hours debate in the House of Commons.
The government has not been entirely honest with the members of this House as to what this money is going to be spent on.
I recall that when I served in another legislature, in a previous life, that it was almost natural for the government to bring in a borrowing authority bill each year. It would give it the right to borrow $1 billion, $2 billion or $3 billion and did not provide even a schedule of the government's borrowing plans and what it planned to spend this money on. We certainly have not seen a schedule tabled in the House as a part of this bill. When we hear the Conservative members speak on this piece of legislation, we do not hear anything as to what the government's plans are in respect of the $25.5 billion that it is borrowing under the authority granted in this bill.
This is the highest level of borrowing authority ever sought from the House of Commons by any government. This is a government that makes a pretence of being fiscally responsible and of being responsible with the public's money. Yet, here it is, on the floor of the House, borrowing the greatest amount that any government has ever come to the House of Commons to seek authority to borrow, without providing a shred of useful information to the members of the House and to the people of Canada, through the members of the House, as to how the money is going to be spent and what it is going to do to benefit the people of Canada.
How can the government expect us to accept a time allocation motion, after four hours debate, on a bill to borrow $25.5 billion? I just cannot understand the government's attitude in this case.
A member from Calgary stood up this morning and told us that this borrowing authority is required to handle social programs. He talked about the family allowance system, the payments to veterans, the old age pensions and supplements. But we were told by an earlier Conservative speaker that the programs of the government are already covered by tax revenues and that in fact the government has a surplus of tax revenues over

program expenditures. So, it does not really need this borrowing authority to cover the programs of government. We would like to know precisely what this $25.5 billion is for.
When I sat in that other legislature and we refused to vote in support of this type of bill, the government was forced to come in with a schedule showing what it intended to spend that money on. Elow can we grant authority to borrow $25.5 billion at the government's discretion, without knowing what the government is going to spend that money on? That is not the duty of a responsible member of Parliament, and we certainly have no intention of doing that.
This bill, which involves $25.5 billion, has been debated for four hours. That is about $6.5 billion per hour and the government is asking us to vote for it without any information at all as to how the money is to be spent. It would be irresponsible for members on this side of the House and members of the House on the opposite side to vote that much authority and credit to the government, at the expense of the people of Canada, without the government telling us what the money is going to be spent on.
We have had different stories from the other side of the House. Some have said it is for social programs. That is completely false because even the Minister of Finance said that the tax revenues of the country cover those social programs. Some have said it is for other reasons, but we simply have not got the accurate information from the government as to what it is going to be spent on. What we need is far more honesty from the government than we have had up to this point if we are going to be expected to support this motion for time allocation, which we do not, and if we are expected to support this borrowing authority, which we cannot as responsible members of the House.
The government acts along the pattern established by Ronald Reagan. It talks lean and mean; it talks about cutting back expenditures; it talks about cutting back debt; and it talks about keeping taxes in line. Yet, the government has been the worst government in history in terms of running up the debt of the country, increasing taxes, and its spending priorities. The government has been one of the worst governments in history. We cannot really be expected, when we see the government follow-
Government Orders
ing the pattern of Ronald Reagan in the United States who was supposed to be the great budget cutter and the great deficit cutter. In fact, he ran up the biggest deficits in the history of the United States, the biggest foreign debt in the history of the United States and made that country the largest debtor country on earth. The Tories here are doing precisely the same thing.
We heard one of the members who spoke this morning say that when the Tories took over the Liberals had run up $160 billion in our national debt. Various speakers on the Tory side then indicated that the debt is now $294 billion, $350 billion, and one person on the opposite side of the House even suggested that the debt is now $380 billion.
This is a government that has increased the debt in six years by more than the debt that all of the governments since Confederation ran up between 1867 and 1984. How can you call that a responsible government? How can you call that a government that is fiscally responsible and that manages the funds of the people of Canada in a fiscally responsible way? This is the government that at the last election called on the electors of Canada and suggested that it was the competent management team. When that program fell flat because people in Canada simply did not believe it, it tried another election strategy. It is definitely not the competent management team. For a team like this to come to the opposition in the House after four hour's debate and ask us to give it the authority to borrow and to spend $25.5 billion, without a shred of evidence as to what they are going to spend it on, is absolutely irresponsible on the part of the government.
I think, Mr. Speaker, you are asking me to wind up my remarks. I simply want to say that we have no intention of supporting the time allocation and that is the position of this party.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1990-91 ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-65
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am speaking today on this time allocation motion and I am going to say categorically, shame on the government. This is the thirty-fifth time, I believe, that we have had stifled democracy. Democracy, to the gentlemen and ladies from across the way, is allowing people to speak their minds, allowing them the benefit of listening to them, and also of speaking to them and explaining to them what is happening.

March 29, 1990
Government Orders
In the eyes of the government, democracy is "do it my way, or the highway". I have news for them. Maybe it should go back to take a lesson in political science. I thought democracy was everyone having a chance to be free and to speak their minds without any fear of being stopped. This is a stifling of democracy. Why? Because the government wants permission to borrow $25.5 billion more without any explanations whatsoever. It says: "Trust me, and I will do great things for you."
The recent polls have told us that people of Canada do not believe the government. They are not trusting the government. They are wanting answers, concrete answers. What will it do with this $25.5 billion? Why does it have to borrow $25.5 billion?
Today we know the interest rates are up, and tomorrow the government will tell us: "We have a larger deficit than was expected because we did not expect the interest rates to go up so high." Why will it not allow us the benefit of judging whether or not the $25.5 billion that it wants is rooted in fact or in just plain needing the money and wanting to have a slush fund.
We all understand that borrowing authority means going to the banks and they give a credit limit. But when governments get that credit limit, it is used up. How many times have we heard of somebody not asking for a higher credit limit, especially when it is government? But tomorrow, you and I and everyone else is going to hear about how expensive it is to borrow that money. Not only is it expensive to borrow that money, but the government is going to bring in a goods and services tax which will create inflation and Mr. Crow will insist on holding tight on his high interest policy. Again, the long term debt will increase because interest rates are higher. When will the government stop hiding, come forward and do something positive for the Canadian people? Tell us, if the government really needs the $25 billion and it is legitimate, why not tell us? Why impose closure?
I have a very difficult time with closure all the time. To me, closure says that the government is anxious about its popularity. It thinks that the less we speak about it, the more quickly it will go away. Well, things do not go away. The people of Canada live today, watch television, read newspapers, and they are better educated and concerned. They will not believe the fairy tale stories any more. No one believes that we will happy tomorrow, that
the GST will solve all our problems, or, for that matter, that this past budget has solved all our problems.
Everyone understands that when the burden is passed on to the next level of government, that level has very little choice. It has either to raise taxes or to pass it down. The municipalities have no choice. They go to then-ratepayers and increase taxes. Those people understand the cost of paying their water rates and their taxes when they increase.
There are a large number of people today facing very, very difficult years ahead. They are living on fixed incomes. Municipal taxes are increasing, water rates are increasing and now heating bills will increase because the GST will impose a terribly harsh burden on hydro bills and gas bills.
Has the government listened to people when they have said: "Listen, we cannot afford to pay the 12 per cent more"? Absolutely not. The government turns a deaf ear and wants to know what it will do. Because some people own big houses and it would not want them to get a break on their heating bills. The government is very willing to give a break to the large corporations. The large corporation is going to get a tax rebate on its heating bill, but the average homeowner is not going to get that break.
If one works for a large corporation and has an expense account, one will be able to go to the Dome, rent a room, have a private party and the company will be able to claim tax input credits. Everything will be all rosy for those people because they are big business. Big business is great and we have to keep encouraging it. We have to give them all the breaks. What about the little guy at the bottom who pays the tune? He is the one who has to pay the bill and he only has two pockets. It is the municipal pocket, the income tax pocket, the GST pocket, or the sales tax pocket, but he only brings in so much money. When the pocket is empty, it is empty.
I implore members of the government to have some consideration and to take the plugs out their ears. The people of Canada are imploring them. It is their future, their country. Would they please stop stifling debate? Would they please start explaining to people? Not only does the government stifle debate, but it does not explain to people what it is doing. Be honest, be upfront. Tell people: "This is what I have to do". It may not be the best thing in the world for you, but I think the people of
March 29, 1990

Government Orders
Canada can understand that there are times when it is necessary to borrow money. But tell us why.
Mr. Speaker, if your wife went out and borrowed money, I would think that you would want to know why. You would want to know what the heck she was going to spend the money on. It would have to be good. It is only normal. I see you agreeing that, yes, she had better. Well, that is what I am saying to the government. This government has to tell me why it is borrowing that money.

For five years now the government has been busy getting our economy ready to face international competition. Piece by piece we have erected better structures to promote economic growth and job creation.

Who is going to be affected negatively? The unemployed, the people who need help, the workers, those who are called upon to retrain because of the massive changes in our society. One can see this government's values, beliefs, and priorities by examining its actions.
Let us look at literacy. We have in this country roughly five million functionally illiterate Canadians, people who do not read or write well enough to be able to give as
much to this society as they would or withdraw from it what they could. It is costing Canada perhaps $10 billion to $11 billion per year.

Let us look at student aid. There have been no changes in criteria since 1984. The cost of living has gone up significantly since then and the cost of education has gone up even higher and more quickly than the regular cost of living.
What has been done? Not only have there been no increases, an administrative fee of 3 per cent has been added on. What is the logic behind adding an administrative fee of 3 per cent to those who need money, to those who have to borrow in order to continue their education. It seems to me that that is totally contradictory to what ought to be done. I mean if you are poor, you ought not to have to pay more in order to pursue an education and a career.
Let us look at research and development. You will recall that the government was going to double the investment. It is roughly half. It has slipped since 1984. We were told to factor out the military. I looked at that because the minister tried to make that point in the House the other day. I looked at the situation and verified that we would still be in sixth place. So let us cut out the com.
Who is affected? All of Canada. All Canadians are affected by the breaking of that promise. Who is affected mostly? Our young men and women, some of our brightest, who contribute most to this country. All of industry, all of society will be affected negatively by the government's actions.
Quite apart from all of those reductions and quite apart from what it says about the beliefs and the values and the priorities, let us look at what else the government has imposed. The costs of the goods and services tax, education, and the postal subsidies will be absorbed. That means that people will be penalized even more. PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   FISHERIES PROTECTION OF HALIBUT
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should protect the halibut fishery off the British Columbia coast from overfishing and ensure adequate stock enhancement by all responsible countries.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the terms of the International Halibut Fishery Commission govern the allocation and the security of this endangered species on the west coast. It is an example of the way in which the fisheries have been managed on both coasts by this government and by its predecessor. At the moment I am concerned and talking about the halibut off the west coast of British Columbia.
In recent years there has been a growing problem with respect to this halibut fishery, namely, that the U.S. troll operations operating out of Alaska have increased to the point that the very future of the fishery itself may well be threatened. This is not a new story about fisheries in Canada.
I refer to the information put forward by the International Pacific Halibut Commission which indicates quite dramatically the direction the catch limits on halibut are in fact going. There is a table put out by the commission called the "IPHC Staff Regulatory Proposals, 1989" in millions of pounds. Most of the material is about area 2: 2A in Washington, 2B in B.C., 2C, 3A, 3B and 4 in Alaska.

March 29, 1990
Private Members' Business
The 1988 catch limit totalled 74.15 million pounds. The 1989 staff recommendations were 64.65 million pounds. The projected future catch limits sets out the same story as we are hearing on the east coast with respect to cod: each year the catch limit is going down. For 1990 the total catch limit is 55.8 million pounds, and for 1991 it will be 47 million pounds.
The commission recognizes that the stocks are being depleted rapidly and is suggesting lower quotas year by year, rather than biting the bullet and making a significant reduction in one year in the hope that the stocks will rebuild.
These figures include the total recreational, treaty Indian and other commercial fisheries.
The origins of many of the problems that have led to the figures I have given can be traced to a 1980 treaty signed between Canada and the U.S. which prohibits the harvesting of halibut in U.S. waters by Canadian fishermen and vice versa. A system for division of the catch was based upon historical catch data held by the IPHC. In area 2, which is from Cape Spencer in northern B.C. to the State of Washington-a lot of water-the Canadian share was set at 60 per cent. The U.S. share was supposed to be 40 per cent of the halibut catch.
There is a chart available again from the same source, the IPHC, which shows that we have not been able to harvest 60 per cent of the total catch in any single year since these records have been kept. In 1984 we came close: between 58 per cent and 59 per cent of the total catch was harvested by B.C. fishermen. It went down to 51.72 per cent in 1985 and to 50 per cent in 1986. There was a bit of a recovery in 1987 when it went up to 51.13 per cent. It went down to 51.52 per cent in 1988 and to 49.7 per cent in 1989. In 1990 it is projected at 49.4 per cent. In 1991 it is projected at 49.2 per cent.
Each year the catch and the projections are going lower and lower. We are getting further and further away from the agreement that we would be able to harvest 60 per cent of the total catch.
One of the major concerns has been that any increase in effort in Alaska, which has been occurring, will seriously affect the harvesting sector in B.C. due to the fact that the migration of halibut from Alaskan waters is interrupted.
Since 1984 there has been a higher than normal abundance of halibut in the Alaskan 2C area. The Alaskan harvesting sector was able to justify an allocation higher than prescribed by the quota due to this abundance.
In 1989, with the halibut stock declining in the 2C area, the Canadian fishermen were still denied the 60 per cent allocation due to the declining stocks in total. The question immediately comes to mind: What is the situation with respect to the total halibut stock?
The viability of the nursery beds was once threatened by the presence of Japanese draggers. Once again this reminds me of what is happening on the east coast with respect to bottom fish stocks.
The U.S. and Canada jointly applied in the 1960s to force Japanese trailers to stop dragging on the more sensitive halibut habitat in the Bering Sea, long before the 200-mile limit ever became law in the late 1970s. The Japanese heavy bottom draggers were tearing up important rearing grounds, which meant they not only slaughtered younger generations of halibut that live to be 30 to 40 years old. but they also ruined feeding and spawning habitat for future generations. The Japanese had to be stopped to protect the species, and they finally were.
As I said, this is the story I kept hearing in Newfoundland and in the Atlantic areas generally about what could be one of the main problems with respect to the cod stocks in those areas.
The viability of the nursery beds were being threatened by the Japanese draggers. They have been expelled. They agreed to be expelled.
Now it is the U.S. dragger fleet that is operating. Regardless of whatever initiatives are taken by the U.S. to monitor activities on the nursery beds or other activities of the U.S. fleet, such as the observer program, the available data indicates that the stock is in serious trouble. According to a submission to the Standing Committee on Forestry and Fisheries in April 1989, it is the same fleet which with the permission of the Alaskan authorities overfished the king crab stock to the point of extinction in the late 1970s to the early 1980s.
Incredibly the information provided by IPHC scientists is that 50 per cent of the damage done to the juvenile halibut stocks is being done on the nursery grounds by the U.S. dragger fleet. In spite of knowing what is the situation, there is a current construction program which
March 29, 1990

will see put in place in the course of 1989 and 1990 an additional 62 new Alaskan factory trailers.
The by-catch by the U.S. trawlers has been estimated by the International Pacific Halibut Commission scientists to amount to 17 million pounds annually or 7 million more than the legal Canadian quota in the 2B area, which area extends from the U.S. border in the south to beyond central B.C. Again there is a problem with respect to the ability or the willingness of the U.S. regulators to restrict their activity.
There is also the question of the illegal Japanese market. If I may quote from the United Fishermen and Allied Workers Union brief of April 1989, it states:
Bob Alverson, the U.S. government appointee to the north Pacific Fisheries Council, was recently astonished to find that before the legal halibut fishery even commenced in May, the four million pound plus Japanese market for under 20 pound halibut has been filled. This illegal trade is supplied almost totally by the U.S. domestic troll fleet.
The United Fishermen and Allied Workers Union set out seven recommendations in its brief. They are that, first, Canada must act immediately to ensure that the U.S. establish regulations prohibiting U.S. trailers from dragging on the more sensitive halibut nursery and rearing grounds.
The second recommendation is that the Canadian government give all possible aid to appropriate private or government groups from Canada and the U.S. which are attempting to lower halibut by-catch limits dramatically in the Bering Sea downward from the current 5,300 tonne limit.
The third recommendation states that American authorities establish a 100 per cent observer program to regulate strictly the U.S. domestic troll fleet. Nothing less will be sufficient.
Fourth, a public investigation into the illegal supply of halibut to Japanese and/or other markets should take place and that corrective measures be taken immediately-
Private Members' Business
Fifth, the United States should compensate Canadian industry for any loss occurring as a result of illegal and/or negligent activity and covered by any such investigation.
The sixth is that the U.S. government move to establish penalties harsh enough to deter law-breakers and to bring them quickly to justice.
Finally, the UFAWU recommends that there is adherence to the Canada-U.S. halibut agreement calling for a Canadian share at the rate of 60 per cent of area 2 quotas.
It is a serious matter. The halibut stock is in danger from overfishing by the U.S. fleets.
The Canadian government, in its Speech from the Throne in April of last year, declared that one of its major concerns was the extent of overfishing which was destroying our domestic industry. This motion will provide all members the opportunity to express themselves in support of an initiative to combat overfishing.
The overfishing endangering the halibut fishery is but one more example of the neglect which has been occurring in respect of the future of this B.C. fishery, as well as of the Atlantic fishery.
I invite all members to support this motion and take this opportunity to demonstrate on this international issue that the Canadian government stands with the fishermen on the west coast in their fight to preserve this Canadian fishery resource for Canadians.
This is a resolution that I think all members of the House could support. It is not criticizing the government. It is asking the government to take action to save a Canadian resource for Canadians. I invite all members to support this motion.

one of the most delightful treats that we have on the west coast. I think that it is a product and a stock that we do need to look after.
What I would like to do is review the halibut industry on the west coast and how it has developed. My colleague has very ably done that to some degree.
Halibut is one of the oldest fisheries in the north Pacific. Well back in our native history we see references to the halibut and the significance that it had in the early days before the white man appeared on the west coast.
While salmon and herring are highly cyclical, halibut, as our colleague pointed out, live much longer. They are not as mobile, although they do range over the north Pacific. It was mentioned that these fish live to 30 or 40 years and arrive at several hundred pounds in that lifetime.
In spite of that we are seeing a decline in the numbers of halibut that we are catching on the west coast. I think the important thing is to pinpoint the reason for this. If indeed overfishing is a significant factor, then we should certainly be changing our quotas, and certainly be negotiating with the Americans to make sure that this very valuable stock is being cared for.
There is also some suggestion that the climatic changes and water temperature changes on the west coast do have an effect on the spawning and on the movement of the halibut. As was pointed out, they do move from American into Canadian waters at various times in their life cycle, so it is important to remember that this is an international problem that we are facing.
It was during the 1930s that the halibut fishing industry took a tremendous growth. It experienced substantially increased landings. Following a catch of 44 million pounds in 1931, annual landings of Pacific halibut rose steadily, peaking at a record 75 million pounds in 1962.
During those early years of the 1960s it became very clear that the resource had been overexploited and halibut landings took a sharp downward turn. In the next 12 years these landings plummeted to a low of only 21 million pounds. This figure includes the American catch as well as the Canadian catch in 1974.
As was pointed out, this was following a prolonged period of foreign fishing and low recruitment. The whole
Pacific halibut fishery declined not only because of local overfishing but because the international fleet was overfishing well. The greatest reductions were off British Columbia and Kodiak Island where the foreign trawling had been most intense and prolonged.
In 1979 Canada and the United States extended their territorial limit to 200 miles. After several years of greatly reduced harvesting and stock rebuilding, the harvest levels recovered and the annual landings rose rapidly.
Although the landings in all areas recovered substantially between 1980 and 1987, the sharpest increases have occurred in the Gulf of Alaska. Again, my colleague has referred to the amount of fishing that has been going on.
During those years, between the 1950s and 1960s, the price of halibut was very stable, but as the presence of halibut declined, the prices increased which again encouraged overfishing. In 1980, however, the price of halibut fell again faster than it had risen in the 1970s. As a result the prices declined to what they were in the 1930s. Adding to the decline in the prices was the expanding growth and efficiency of the halibut fleet resulting in a shorter fishing season and less product sold in the higher priced fresh fish market.
On the west coast of Canada the halibut fisheries spans 500 miles. It always has played an important role in the commercial fishery in British Columbia.
Prior to the signing of the extended jurisdiction in 1977 and the implementation of the 200-mile limit in 1979, vessels from both nations fished halibut off each other's coasts. Similarly, the fishing fleets of each nation shared in the good and bad times of the halibut fishery.
Since 1979 and 1980 Canadian and U.S. vessels have been restricted to fishing in the waters within their own national jurisdiction. This has had a tremendous effect on the B.C. halibut fleet because we no longer have the opportunity to fish up in the Bering Sea where there are
2,000	miles of coastline to fish. We are now limited to the 500-mile area off the B.C. coast.
These limitations have had one beneficial effect in that the Canadian government has been able to better control the fishery. It also prevented the Canadian
March 29, 1990

fishermen from sharing in the boom of the 1980s in the Gulf of Alaska.
Between 1979 and 1983, B.C. halibut landings hovered around the 5 million pound level. After 1983, landings have risen steadily and reached 12.9 million pounds in 1988.
Although the increase in the harvest level was good news to Canadian fishermen, catches were increasing even more rapidly in the Alaskan fisheries where substantially larger quantities of halibut are landed. Quota increases were implemented several years later. We recognize that this may not necessarily be due to increased stocks but perhaps to the increased fishing effort.
In 1981, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans limited the growth in the number of fishing vessels in the commercial halibut fishery by cutting the number of licences issued to form a limited entry fishery. Approximately 440 halibut licences were issued to Canadian fishing vessels. It should be noted that not all vessels with a halibut licence participate in the halibut fishery each and every year.
In the mid-1980s, the number of fishing boats was between 301 and 337. Because of the increasing value of the halibut since 1984, in 1988 all 435 licences were renewed.
By 1987, virtually all commercial fishing vessels with halibut fishing privileges were actively fishing halibut. The fishing capacity continued to increase. The Canadian fleet was able to catch in excess of 12 million pounds in a mere 16 fishing days.
In 1989 Canadian fishermen were permitted to fish only one eight-day period and one three-day period. This was largely due to technological changes in the gear and equipment, such as circle hooks, snap-on gear, automatic baiting machines and improved fish finding electronics. This increased the efficiency to levels that had been entirely unheard of and unthought of just five years earlier. The result of these changes was a halibut fleet which in 1987 harvested over twice the catch in nearly one-quarter of the time required in 1982.
As has been pointed out, the changes in halibut fleet catching power were most dramatic in the unlimited entry fishery in the Gulf of Alaska where, in 1987, 30 million pounds of halibut were caught in less than two
Private Members' Business
days. This of course is one of the real concerns of the halibut fishery on the west coast.
In recent years the halibut fishery in the Gulf of Alaska has taken the allowable catch limit, also in a few days, even though recent annual catches are nearing historical highs. For comparison, the 1988 Gulf of Alaska catch limit of 55.5 million pounds was taken in five days and three days, subject to limits on the amount of halibut which may be landed by each vessel, whereas in the late 1970s over 40 days were required to take the annual catch limits of less than 20 million pounds.
The Canadian fishery, which is smaller in size and has limited entry licensing, has also realized substantial increases in catchability and sharp decreases in the numbers of fishing days.
In 1979 the Canadian fleet landed less than 5 million pounds in 40 unrestricted days and in 1988 caught 12.5 million pounds in 13 fishing days.
In 1990 fishermen may choose to fish a four-day period in April or a four-day period in June. The remaining total allowable catch can be taken in a clean-up fishery in September.
The total allowable catch this year is 7.8 million pounds. These shorter fishing seasons are the result of new fishing technology, increased efficiency and, in the case of the United States, increases in the number of vessels.
Declining halibut stocks off the B.C. coast are probably due in part to overfishing, but we need to do much more research into the causes of the decline of the fishery. If there are climatic changes, changes in the sea bed or drift-net fishing, then I agree the Canadian government should certainly take a firm stand in these areas.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   FISHERIES PROTECTION OF HALIBUT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for giving me this opportunity to support the motion before the House which calls for the protection of the British Columbia halibut fishery from overfishing and the maintenance of adequate stock enhancement by all responsible countries.
For the information of the House, halibut is a migratory stock which spawns in specific spawning areas in British Columbia and Alaska. They migrate south and east. The migration brings them into the fishing grounds of British Columbia and the states of Alaska and

March 29, 1990
Private Members' Business
Washington. It is here that they become available for the long-line fisheries harvest.
There is also an important rearing ground for the halibut fishery in the Bering Sea. This area nurtures the fish which can live to be 30 to 40 years old and weigh up to 500 pounds.
In the 1960s it was discovered that the Japanese trailers were dragging this area and tearing up the feeding and spawning halibut. The Canadian and Americans, under the auspices of the International Pacific Halibut Commission, IPHC, succeeded in stopping the Japanese dragging in this area after intense international pressure was applied.
Today, however, the Americans and Canadians operate under the 1980 treaty which prohibits Canadians from harvesting in American waters and vice versa. The treaty negotiated in good faith was based upon the assumption that the two nations which fought so hard to preserve the halibut stocks would act responsibly in their own fishing grounds. This did not turn out to be the case. The Japanese have been replaced by the Americans who are now trolling the nursing grounds.
One advantage of having fishermen fish in each other's waters was that each nation would have a vested interest in ensuring that the stocks were healthy along the entire migratory route. The Americans, in particular the Alaskans, decided to take advantage of this situation. The Alaskans realized that the fish migrated from the Bering Sea through the waters of Alaska, British Columbia and Washington, in that order. Therefore, they would always have the first grab at the stocks.
From this situation the Alaskan fishing fleet grew dramatically to approximately 4,300 vessels. This is roughly 10 times the size of our fleet in British Columbia. Not only is the fleet huge but it is largely unregulated. Therefore, it is difficult to detect overfishing.
The IPHC has known about this situation for several years but has consistently been unable to persuade the Americans to institute observers on all their vessels. This is annoying to the Canadian fisheries industry which each year helps to stock and conserve the species but continues to find its catch declining in volume.
In 1989, new and alarming statistics came to light regarding the overfishing by the Americans. Here are just a few examples. The Alaskan Fishermen's Journal reported that the southeastern Alaskan troll fishery catch of targeted flounder was less than one-quarter the value of the prohibited halibut and crab taken in the fishery.
IPHC scientists estimated that the incidental by-catch of halibut by the U.S. trailers amounted to 17 million pounds, which was 7 million pounds more than the total allowable catch for Canada in 1988. These figures were later determined to be too low.
The IPHC scientists also believe that 50 per cent of the stock damage done to juvenile halibut stocks is done right on the sensitive nursery grounds. Given these alarming statistics, we must further study methods which will enable us to protect our common halibut nursery grounds and also deter the Alaskans from overfishing and trolling the nursery grounds.
Further to this, it is of the utmost importance that we enlist the help of Americans in this matter. A unilateral Canadian action in this matter is futile without the co-operation of all parties involved in the international halibut fishery.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to congratulate the member for Nanaimo- Cowichan for bringing this resolution to the floor of the House and also congratulate the other speakers who have intervened in this motion.
It is very important, from the point of view of the Pacific Coast fishery, that Parliament resolve on this issue and take a strong stand. It is very important to the people on the west coast who have already seen what has happened in the east coast fishery as a result of competing fleets taking more and more of the resource and less and less attention being paid to conservation of that resource. We have seen serious damage done to the fish stocks off the east coast and serious damage done to the economies with fish plants shutting down in a number of towns throughout the Atlantic provinces.
I used to work in the fishing industry in British Columbia back when I was going to university and high school. I worked in a shipyard in Richmond, B.C. owned by Nelson Brothers Fisheries Limited. I recall when the boats came back from the Gulf of Alaska and the Bering Sea they used to bring for the workers in the shipyard huge halibut that they had caught in the Bering Sea and
March 29, 1990

in the Gulf of Alaska. It was my job as somebody who worked in the shipyard to go down in the hold of these big fishing vessels to put a block on these halibut and lift them up so that they could be cut into chunks for the shipyard workers. When those halibut were standing on end with the blocks they used to be eight to ten feet high.
In recent years, the number and size of halibut has declined dramatically. We are concerned on the west coast of Canada that this fish is being fished to extinction by bad management, not necessarily bad management within Canadian waters and by Canadian authorities but definitely bad management in the state of Alaska and in the United States where the prime nursery grounds for the halibut reside.
I hope that this resolution will give strength to our government negotiators and strength to our government in negotiating with the United States, with the government of the state of Alaska and with Alaskan fishermen to try to change the attitude that those fishermen and that those jurisdictions have with respect to the nursery beds of the Pacific halibut.
If we do not protect those nursery beds from which the halibut originate and spread in their migratory patterns throughout the balance of the west coast, as other members have mentioned, we are going to lose these fish altogether. Anybody who has tasted Pacific halibut will know that it is one of the highest quality and value fish that we get off the west coast, second only to our salmon and herring. Again, I would like to congratulate the members who have spoken on this issue.
The problem is that the United States fishery in the Gulf of Alaska and in those critical halibut nursery areas are virtually unregulated. That is the same fishery as was mentioned by previous speakers that fished the Alaska king crab to extinction. What they are doing now is the equivalent of what was discussed several years ago in the Atlantic coast fishery. What they are doing is pulse fishing. As they fish one species to extinction, then they go on to the next species and fish them to extinction. We have to ask ourselves, when they finish with the halibut, what is the next species in line for extinction on the west coast of Canada?
Private Members' Business
This is an extremely important issue. I know that government members, official opposition members and New Democratic Party members are fully in agreement on this issue. I hope that the House will resolve itself in order to give government the authority and the voice of Parliament when it is negotiating with the United States on this issue so that we can come up with a fairer allocation of the fishery between Canada and the United States and also more appropriate methods of protecting the nursery grounds for halibut in the Gulf of Alaska and the Bering Sea so that we do not lose the halibut fishery entirely on the west coast of British Columbia.
We do not need one more species fished to extinction by bad management or by neglect in the discussions and the relations between Canada and the United States. I think on this one, Parliament should give the government the authority to take a very strong stand with the state of Alaska, a very strong stand with the Government of the United States and a very strong stand with American fishermen to let them know loudly and clearly that we would like to see this fishery preserved and that we would like to see this fish brought back from the verge of extinction.
