speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to speak to the subject matter of Motion M-305, and more specifically to the concerns of the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowi-chan (Mr. Stupich) regarding the development of halibut stocks.
I would like to take a few minutes to talk about a development program that is a little better known on the Pacific coast, and I am referring to the Salmonid Enhancement Program. The program, a welcome federal-provincial project, was launched in 1977 to double salmonid stocks on the Pacific coast and bring them back to pre-1900 levels. The program was also designed to raise national income levels, create jobs, help remote coastal communities, enhance the well-being of Native peoples, and preserve and protect the environment. The program includes construction and operation of hatcheries, spawning and nursery channels, fish ladders and incubators. It applies techniques including improving habitat, stocking lakes and the use of aquaculture to raise five species of salmonids and anadromous rainbow trout.

March 29, 1990
Private Members' Business
The Salmonid Enhancement Program is expected to produce nearly one-third of salmonid production in British Columbia in the course of the last decade of the twentieth century. Is the hon. member suggesting that the program be expanded to include other species such as halibut? We must realize there are significant differences between the life cycles of salmon and halibut that would make it difficult to apply this enhancement program to halibut.
Pacific halibut is a flat ground fish that may grow to a very large size. In the northern Pacific, halibut is found from Southern California to the Bering Sea. It generally lives in deep waters, especially during the winter when it goes to its spawning grounds off the continental shelf. Halibut prefer cold waters with temperatures varying from 3 to 8 degrees Celsius and have been found at depths of up to 1,100 meters.
The halibut's life cycle starts with tiny eggs freely floating in water. Fertilization is external, and the eggs hatch about two weeks later. The larvae start feeding on zooplankton when their vitellus has been absorbed.
During the first four or five months, juvenile halibut are carried by deep ocean currents. As the larvae mature, their specific gravity decreases. They rise to the surface and drift towards shallow waters on the continental shelf. Many are carried north by the Alaska current to the Gulf of Alaska, the Aleutian Islands and as far as the Bering Sea.
A halibut undergoes significant physical changes in the first six months. Ordinary-looking at first, it gradually changes into a typical flat fish with the eyes located on the upper side of the body.
That is when the fish begins to live in relatively shallow breeding grounds less than 61 metres along the continental shelf where it will remain for about three years, feeding on shrimp and fry.
At age three, halibuts seek deeper waters and a good many of them travel in a southeasterly direction, the opposite of their first migration towards the northeast as larvae. Some have been know to migrate over distances in excess of 6,000 kilometres. Halibuts coming back to B.C. waters are usually five or six years old. Data recorded from tags indicate that migratory stocks mix together and that no distinct population has been noted.
Male halibuts reach maturity at age eight, as compared to age 12 for female halibuts. The latter grow more rapidly and live longer than males do. A halibut weighing more than 45 kilograms is usually female. Specimens weighing up to 227 kilograms have been reported but the average weight of halibut caught on an ordinary fishing line ranges roughly from 14 to 18 kilograms and in an 8-to-12 age bracket. The halibut's known longevity record is 27 years for males and 42 years for females.
The halibut spawns in winter-November to March- at depths ranging from 270 to 400 metres. Spawning grounds have been spotted over wide coastal areas, but we know they are found primarily in British Columbia, Cape St. James, Langara Island and Frederick Island. Goose Island, Hecate Strait and Rose Spit are other known spawning grounds. Females lay a huge number of eggs and fecundity depends on the size of the fish.
Successful stock replenishment also depends on natural abundance cycles which seem to recur every 20 years. Halibut catches are beginning to decrease after several years of record production, so obviously the species will decline over the next few years and halibut landings are bound to be smaller than they have been in recent years.
Accidental young halibut catches are a major cause of mortality, particularly in waters off the Alaskan coast. Contrary to the larger size halibut which prefers to stay in a definite area, younger halibut less than 65 centimetres in lengh travel a lot and may be captured in many fisheries. Younger halibuts have a high growth potential and their mortality rate resulting from accidental catches may reduce significantly the strength of the mature halibut stocks over the following years.
The Government of Canada is concerned about the high mortality rate of the young halibut population resulting from trawl fishing. It should be recognized that last year the accidental catches were somewhat higher than over the past five years. The assessment of accidental catches over the 5 to 10 previous years was 1.5 higher. Canada is asking the United States to implement a conservation program and a monitoring program. I think this is one of the points which will interest my Hon. friend.
March 29, 1990

The United States have recognized the legitimacy of our concerns and support our requests for a stricter implementation program. Other initiatives such as the imposition of quotas per outing, a controlled access, changes to fishing gears, the restriction of over fishing areas and seasons, as well as the closing of spawning grounds are being considered.
As I mentioned earlier, most of the salmon stock enhancement techniques are being used in the shallow fresh water spawning grounds before the prococious parrs start their migration towards the sea where they will mature. Halibut, as I said, has quite a different biological cycle.
Salmons return to fray in the shallow water of the coastal rivers and lakes, while halibuts spawn in deep sea water. It is therefore difficult to implement enhancement activities for the halibut, a pelagic species. The same comparison applies to rearing habitats. The salmon's environment can be modified to a certain extent in fresh water, for instance by restocking lakes, in order to increase productivity but halibut rearing habitats cannot be changed.
Halibut incubation is possible and research is under way in this area. However, this technology is not advanced enough for large-scale application and there is no guarantee that efforts will lead to more abundant halibut stocks for Canadian fishermen. The future of these stocks rests with fishery managers who, as it has already been said, can take certain steps to preserve stocks and make sure that our fishermen benefit from the abundant renewable natural resources in British Columbia waters.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to assure my hon. colleague that the government objective is to protect halibut stocks in the Pacific as well as other Canadian fish stocks. In dealing with this situation, the Canadian government is working closely with our neighbours to the south, the United States, to conclude agreements aimed at protecting halibut stocks in the Pacific while ensuring a fishing activity which will allow many British Columbia communities to benefit from the economic spin-offs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege for me to speak this afternoon on the motion put forward by
Private Members' Business
my friend across the way from British Columbia. I am used to speaking in this House on fisheries matters that tend to pertain more to the east coast and so it is nice to have the opportunity to speak on a matter which is of particular importance to western Canada, to British Columbia.
The fishery in British Columbia is very different from the fishery we have in Atlantic Canada and certainly right now it does not face the same nature or level of problems that we face. Nevertheless, it is important that we not totally forget that the industry in British Columbia is a very important employer in a number of communities along the coast on Vancouver Island, particularly in the native communities. There is a thriving commercial fishery certainly in the context that I know it, a very strong recreational fishery, a commercial recreational fishery, a native fishery that is booming and seeing some real innovation.
The attention of the government of Canada must be maintained in that area. They too have problems. Quite often their problems are problems that we would love to have as they are more problems of allocation of resources, whereas ours on the east coast tend to be in finding the resources that we could allocate. We would certainly have no trouble in allocating fish, Mr. Speaker, I am sure you can imagine, if it were there.
The question of halibut has been discussed quite ably here this afternoon. There are a number of aspects to it. I would like to concentrate if I could on one that is of particular concern. My friends from the New Democratic Party have alluded to the Atlantic Pacific Halibut Commission. It is the organization that governs halibut and governs how we in Canada, and to some extent the United States, catch this species. It is a commission established by both governments to deal with the halibut resource in the northeast Pacific. The commission meets annually to establish quotas and to set regulatory measures and the implementation of those regulations and those quotas is up to the governments of each country.
The involvement of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, which is responsible for Canada's role in conservation of fish stocks and also participation in international organizations like the halibut commission, is to ensure that prior to the annual meeting of the commission there is a fair amount of consultation. That consultation is not only focused simply on the particular issue of the annual

March 29, 1990
Private Members' Business
meeting of the commission, and it has an annual meeting of the Canadian participants in the fishery in advance, but also an ongoing consultation throughout the year to deal with issues that may or may not arise on a variety of things such as juvenile mortality, incidental by-catches, particularly in the Alaskan groundfish troll. We have heard a fair bit about that. It is a problem. It is something in which the DFO is involved with the industry, the unions and a number of others.
One of the most important things DFO is trying to do in consultation with the industry and discussions with those involved is to deal with the competitive intensity that we see in the industry. This has moved us more and more to shorter fishery openings. This has caused a problem that I would like to talk about. The intensity of the catch, the intensity of the season is a concern that we have for a number of reasons: the effect it has on the industry, the effect it has on conservation, and the effect it has generally on our ability to produce good quality fish considering the focus of the opening of the season and the intensity that follows from that.
We have seen a huge improvement in technology and larger boats and this enables huge quantities of fish to be caught in very short periods of time. In mere hours, the catch limits are caught. That, in itself, causes a problem. When we catch fish very quickly, we run the risk of not only overfishing but there is a risk of underfishing. The risk of overfishing is very clear because obviously it is in the interests of no one that we catch more than our quota and that is something to be concerned about. At the same time, it is not in the interests of fishermen that we leave fish in the water, that resources be left uncaught, when the allowable catch would have allowed that they be caught and fishermen who depend on every fish that they can catch could have had fish that was left in the frenzy of the season.
Conservation of halibut stocks is particularly important. We have talked about that here today and I think everybody would agree that there has to be a clear focus of a government department responsible for fisheries and this government department is no different. One thing that is a problem is the several millions of pounds of halibut every year which is lost as a result of abandoned gear or of juvenile or under-sized halibut that have to be put back into the water as a conservation method but which we all know is a fairly ineffective conservation method. From time to time there is illegal prospecting going on, where there are catches taken out of season. One of the biggest problems is the short, intense fishing period which heightens all of this.
The current management system reduces the opportunity for fishermen fishing other species. There are many other species that are fished in British Columbia such as salmon, sable fish, Pacific cod, and rock fish. There are halibut catches in those fisheries. There are by-catches and incidental catches. It is important that we and our friends south of the border know that we are managing that, that we are minimizing some of that and ensuring that we do not allow that incidental by-catch and do not maintain those fisheries at the cost of the fishery, generally.
There are some serious marketing difficulties that the Department of Fisheries and Oceans is involved in and which result from this high-intensity season. Clearly, one problem is the availability of high quality fresh fish. Because of the huge numbers of fish caught quite quickly, it is frozen, and with the freezing of fish there is not the availability, at all times, of fresh fish and frozen fish, whether we like it or not, does not make as good a product. As a result, we lose the optimization of the value to fishermen and those in the industry, generally.
Harvesting costs go up as more and more equipment is bought to ensure that the individual fisherman can be as competitive as possible and more crews are hired. One of the other short season problems is the risk that it provides for a fisherman, who perhaps for reasons of ill health, weather, or a breakdown of gear, cannot get into the fishery and prosecute it in that intensely short period of time and he or she may be left out totally. It is also important to recognize the safety concerns.
We have some experience in British Columbia and particularly on the east coast with enterprise allocations. Hon. members are well aware that in the mid seventies the enterprise allocations program in the eastern Canadian cod fishery was developed so that we would avoid this highly competitive and highly intensive attack on the stocks. Frankly, it is in the interests of those in the industry, those who fish and those who work in fish
March 29, 1990

plants. If we can spread the work out over a greater period of time, there is an interest in doing that.
Obviously, what I have said is not going to be supported by everyone. There is much controversy about moving into a limited entry fishery or a more specifically managed fishery. It is something that changes the way things have developed. Obviously, it will affect some enterprises and some fishermen. I do not think the Minister of Fisheries intends to move immediately or quickly on any of these issues. They are issues that are important to discuss as we look at the conservation.

speechtext:
Well, if he does it will be to the credit of the hon. member for St. John's East who has always had the interests of fishermen at heart.
As a matter of fact, last summer, the hon. member for St. John's East invited me to his riding and around Newfoundland to visit the fisheries. Together we went to visit fishermen to hear first-hand their interests. He thought it was important for a fellow from the prairies, from the Rocky Mountain province of Alberta, to understand first-hand the concerns of fishermen. It was a great insight for me, as I think it would be for all members. If the hon. member for Kingston who has entered this debate in part today would take the opportunity, I am sure at the invitation of the member for St. John's East, would go and visit the fishery, he would not be so flippant in his remarks about the difficulties the fishermen are experiencing.
I would like to express my pleasure in speaking on the Pacific halibut fishery. Conservation of halibut stocks has been a priority in the administration of the Pacific fishery and will continue to be a priority as the abundance of halibut stocks decline naturally and as the capacity of the fleets to catch halibut grows.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to have the opportunity again to condemn the government for its savage and unthinking cuts to aboriginal communications. Ordinary Canadians throughout the country have reacted with shock and dismay. Aboriginal Canadians are outraged.
What makes these cuts so offensive is the way they were announced, with no warning and no time provided for the aboriginal communications societies to find alternative sources of funding. In addition to the suddenness of the cuts are the inevitable comparisons to what did not get cut in this budget.
The government will be spending millions of dollars on goods and services tax advertising, or propaganda. It bought some stripes for the National Gallery for over $1 million. It wrote off millions in Third World nations' debts but slashed and eliminated funding for aboriginal political organizations and communications.
The government does not comprehend the vital importance of aboriginal communications to aboriginal people. It has blinders on when it comes to languages other than the country's two official languages.
The Prime Minister promised, in 1985, that programs for aboriginal people would not be cut back. Let me quote from the Prime Minister's press release of April 18, 1985:
Current funding levels of programs designed to correct the serious
inequities which exist for native people in native communities will be
maintained.
He went on to say:
Policies regarding aboriginal people will be made after open, public consultation, especially at the grassroots level.
The Prime Minister also said in the same statement that "the special relationship between Canada and the aboriginal people should be strengthened".
All of these beautiful sounding promises and commitments have been broken in the recent budget.
The serious inequities that the Prime Minister mentioned still exist. They have not gone away since 1985. In fact, many of them have been made worse by the government's actions. The rate increase by Canada Post on food mail shipments to northern and remote communities is but one example.
The government's own documents attest to the continuing disparities. Last summer the government released its aboriginal economic development strategy. I will quote some figures from the government's own strategy paper:
By all measures of socio-economic disparity, the 600,000 people who identify themselves as aboriginal continue to be the most disadvantaged group within Canadian society. Employment rates among the aboriginal working-age population have been about 45 percent compared with 63 percent for the non-aboriginal population. Of those employed, incomes are up to a third lower than levels for employed non-aboriginal people.
Almost 30 percent of aboriginal individuals aged 15-24 have less than a grade 9 education, compared with 7 percent per cent for their non-aboriginal counterparts. More than 76 percent have neither completed high school nor pursued post-secondary education, whereas the corresponding percentage for nonaboriginals is 44 percent.
Despite these low education and employment statistics, the government capped post-secondary education funding.
In the area of health, serious inequities persist. A recent report of the Canadian Institute of Child Health confirms the continuing problems.
The aboriginal mortality rate from injuries and suicides, hospitalizations due to respiratory diseases and pregnancy complications remain much higher than the national average. Life expectancy for aboriginal people is still much lower than for non-aboriginal people. Aboriginal children born in the late 1980s will live, on average, 68 years. Other Canadian children can expect to live 76 years.
March 29, 1990

The aboriginal infant mortality rate is double the national average. Aboriginal children have consistently higher death rates due to injuries. Aboriginal teenagers have a suicide rate seven times higher than the total Canadian rate. Tuberculosis and other infectious conditions disproportionately affect aboriginal people.
The Canadian Institute of Child Health report states that "we have a Third World problem within our society" in terms of the health disadvantages of aboriginal children. The pattern of disease among Canada's aboriginal people resembles the main killers of the developing world.
The Prime Minister and the government can hardly argue in the face of all of this evidence that disparities no longer exist between aboriginal people and non-aboriginal people. So why was the funding cut for aboriginal communications and organizations?
As for the consultation promised by the Prime Minister-open public consultation at the grassroots level- there was none. Instead, the government has set up a task force after the cuts were announced. The task force is to assist aboriginal communications societies to diversify their funding and revenue base.
The government totally eliminated the $3.5 million Native Communications Program in the February 20 budget. It slashed funding under the Northern Native Broadcast Access Program by 16 per cent or $2.2 million. A broadcast distribution fund of $800,000 was suspended. All this means a potential loss of 180 jobs, aboriginal jobs in a communications field which is unique and cannot be replaced.
The Canadian Human Rights Commission last year said that Canada's treatment of aboriginal peoples is a national tragedy. Today the Canadian Human Rights Commission said it has no reason to alter its judgment. The commission's press statement of today states:
If there is any single issue on which Canada cannot hold its head
high in the international community, any single area in which we can
be accused of falling down on our obligations, it is in this area of
aboriginal relations.
The minister would be well advised to read the human rights report which was released today.
Adjournment Debate

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since there has been criticism of the budgetary cuts in the native programs administered by the Department of the Secretary of State, I would like to remind members of other quite substantial funds still being made available from that quarter.
Even after a cut of 5 per cent the 99 Friendship Centres serving native people in urban areas will be receiving $17.4 million.
The Aboriginal Representative Organizations Program will still receive $8.2 million in the form of sustaining grants to organizations representing aboriginal people.
The Department of Indian and Northern Affairs which, already gives considerable funds to status Indian organizations, has seen its budgets increase from $1.4 billion in 1984-85 to $2.3 billion in the current year. Another 32 native organizations will still be receiving sustaining grants from the Secretary of State. The funding these organizations receive will be reduced by between 7.5 per cent and 15 per cent. The department will still be providing $11.3 million under the Northern Native Broadcast Access Program to enable native organizations to produce and broadcast on regional radio and TV in the north.
In addition, the department has provided over $1 million in transitional funds to all organizations whose funding was eliminated under the Native Communications Program. This money is to assist the native communications societies in diversifying their funding base.
Finally, the Secretary of State will continue to provide $2.2 million for aboriginal women's programs and $1 million for social and cultural development. These programs are not affected by our restraint measures.
There is no question that the decisions about funding reductions have been difficult ones to make in the Department of the Secretary of State as well as elsewhere, but programs have been preserved which served the neediest client groups. That seems to be the fairest possible way to handle the reductions we must make in government spending.
This principle can be seen at work in other departments. Money and social services goes up $77 million in

March 29, 1990
Adjournment Debate
one year. There will be $59 million more for education. Health services for native people are being given an additional $35 million. The economic development program in Indian and Northern Affairs will get an increase of $93 million, which is 40 per cent in one year. In total, other support is increasing by more than $200 million in a year when government services elsewhere in the country are holding the line or being cut.
Finally, when we look at projected capital expenditures on behalf of native people, we see even more strikingly the high priority given to their needs. As one example among many, the budget allots $592 million for on-reserve facilities and related services, an increase of $28 million over the current year. The government's sustained commitment to the well-being of our aboriginal community and culture is clearly evident. All together, government funding for aboriginal programs will rise to more than $4 billion in 1990-1991.
To conclude, difficult decisions are sometimes needed to solve our deficit problems, but the handling of native programs has been as fair and as a balanced as possible. I am sure we would not want it any other way.

Mr. Francis G. LeBIanc (Cape Breton Highlands -
Canso): Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to have the opportunity to elaborate on the question that I posed the Minister of Fisheries on Thursday last, March 22.
The question had to do with the dumping at sea of large quantities of fish by offshore fishing trawlers. I had made reference to the minister's visit to Canso soon after he assumed his portfolio in late February when he met with a group of trawlermen from Canso, Nova Scotia. The trawlermen presented him with tangible evidence of fish being dumped at sea.
I am not talking about the discarding the fish at sea. That is a current practice in offshore fishing activities, of taking a load of fish in and culling the catch that is brought on board by a trawler. I am talking about another practice, which is dumping the fish at sea. That is the practice of releasing a large quantity of fish caught in the large trawler net. That is a much more wasteful practice and that is the practice which the trawlermen were bringing to the attention of the Minister of Fisheries. They had photographs and other evidence to demonstrate their case.
This is a controversial issue. The offshore fishing companies like National Sea have been denying that large-scale dumping occurs. The government officials of DFO have been denying that large-scale dumping occurs. While they admit that there is some form of discarding that takes place, they say it is a limited degree of high grading, that it is controllable, and that is not happening at an unreasonable rate or at least that they cannot get a handle on it.
We have to understand the position of the trawlermen. These trawlermen go out for nine days with the cloud of the closure of their community and the loss of their jobs over their heads. Their whole livelihood is at stake. The government and the companies are telling them that there are no fish. They are catching vast quantities of fish and are obliged to throw those fish overboard. These are the same fish that could be processed in their community. At the same time, the plant that they fish to is closing its doors.
You can understand the frustration of the trawlermen in Canso, Mr. Speaker, when they brought this to the concerns of the minister. They were frustrated even more when the minister seemed to shuffle-off then-concerns after a month.
I am glad to bring this matter to the attention of the House. I want to advise the House that it is not only the trawlermen at Canso who have raised these concerns. The report of the Senate committee on the marketing of fish in Atlantic Canada recommends that "statements made to the committee by many fishermen indicated that large but unknown quantities of potentially valuable fish were being caught and routinely dumped at sea because they were either too small or incidental to the species sought." These are trawler boats travelling at sea looking for one species, such as cod and get a large quantity of another species. They do not want it so they pitch it overboard. As a result, this fish is wasted.
To give you an example of the extent of this practice, it is as if we finally started bringing oil from Hibernia and dumped two-thirds of the oil back into the ocean. That is the degree of the practice we are talking about.
March 29, 1990

This is a controversial issue and we need more information. First, it is very important that we recognize, as the Senate recommends, the potential seriousness of the issue and we take steps to get the facts.
The Minister of Fisheries should take the matter seriously enough to be willing to get facts to determine the extent to which this is happening. What are the causes? What are the incentives to the companies and to the trawlermen who are allowing this practice to happen.
Second, we have to take a new attitude towards commercial fishing as we have towards other activities such as forestry or manufacturing and view this activity as an environmental activity. Its profound concerns for the environment, commercial fishing and the practices of commercial fish companies have to be subordinate to the broader issue of the environment and the status of our resource.
We will have to bear the cost of taking all the fish we catch and not leave some at sea because that fish is not particularly valuable at that point in time given the market situation.
I will close now and I welcome the response of my colleague opposite to this veiy important issue.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to respond to my hon. friend because he knows of where he speaks and raises an interesting concern.
I am sure he does not suggest that the habit of culling or selective dumping is one that we should encourage. It is abhorrent to dump any resource. There is no question that it goes on. To say that two-third is dumped is a bit out of whack.
I was with the Minister of Fisheries when he was in Canso, Lockeport and Gaultois. I travelled across the country with him. It was clear that the trawlermen who make their living on trawlers are very conscious of conservation. They are very conscious that they are a part of a system that from time to time abuses the resource. They are very specific on that matter.
My friend opposite is right to the extent that officials in the Department of Fisheries say that when there are observers on the ships the discard level is between 2 per cent and 5 per cent. The trawlermen said that when the observers are on the ship the discard levels are about as
Adjournment Debate
observed, but when the observers are not on the ships it is significantly higher.
The Hache Task Force made very clear and the government has agreed that there must be much greater-and I would suggest 100 per cent-observer coverage on the trawlers. My friend talks about information. It is important that the Department of Fisheries and the industry has information on the catch, rapidity of catch, the bi-catch and the times. Those things are important.
The Hache report makes very clear that that is important. I think today on the Scotian shelf, observes cover about 50 per cent. In the North Atlantic fishery it runs about 80 per cent. Northern cod are running 100 per cent. So it balances itself out.
It is incumbent upon the Department of Fisheries- the industry and others will have to be involved-that we move to 100 per cent observer coverage. I hope that addresses the problem.
The minister was very moved by what he saw in Canso. He went to his department as soon as he returned and asked what is going on? He is very conscious of it. I think you will see that in his actions over time as we come to grips with this sort of problem. We cannot under any circumstance condone the waste of this resource, particularly when we are in such difficult situations as we are now.

Mr. Speaker, on February 14 I asked a question of the Minister of Tourism to the effect that the new GST would have a detrimental effect on the tourist industry in this country.
The minister answered that it was not an additional tax facing the tourist industry but the replacement of the old tax.
The fact of the matter is that I could have brought to the House this afternoon countless letters which I have in my office and could table if necessary. These letters concern the difficulties the tourist industry will have with the GST.
I have had calls from travel agencies that tell me it will be very difficult to package tours from the United States into Canada because each individual tourist from the United States or from other countries in the world who come to Canada will have to make out individual rebate

March 29, 1990
Adjournment Debate
slips. People who come to visit this country do not want to do paperwork.
I would like my hon. friend who will answer these questions if he has elaborated the special rebate? It was supposed to be a global rebate rather than individual tourists filling out a rebate slip. I would like to know if there are any developments in that regard.
Some of the letters I have received mention the fact that if a tourist comes to Canada and does not spend a minimum of $300, be it in restaurants or buying a gift, they cannot have a rebate. Statistics have shown that the tourists coming to this country from the United States when adding up their restaurant bills and money spent on small gifts or souvenirs may not reach the minimum because people who watch their spending are going to be very sensitive to the additional 7 per cent tax.

I will be brief, Mr. Speaker, because I do not wish to make the question too long for my hon. colleague opposite who has to answer it. Ele will understand that the tourist industry has had rough times in the last two years. Let us not get into the causes. There may be many reasons why tourism has gone through some difficulties in Canada.
I would submit that the Minister of Tourism should make the Minister of Finance aware of the fact that this tax, as its stands, will certainly cause problems for the organizations and the people who organize tours of our country for visitors from all over the world, which are commonly called package tours.
You will therefore understand the concerns expressed by the Tourism Industry Association of Canada in the letter I received from them, among others. As a matter of fact, they came here on February 11 or 12, or was it the 14. I do not remember the exact date. They have voiced numerous times their concerns regarding this tax and were not satisfied with the answers they were given.
Essentially, based on all the letters and all the phone calls I have received, the tourist industry is asking if it would be possible to get a rebate. The businesses would like to know if the companies organizing tours, be it in a given province or across Canada, for a week, two weeks or a month, could themselves apply an overall rebate. That way, each visitor from outside the country could benefit from that rebate. If that were allowed, the package tours from all over the United States would not be affected by the tax. That is perhaps one of the concerns expressed by the industry. There are many more, but this is one of them.
I will have the opportunity, in the weeks to come, to elaborate further on the questions I asked the minister of Tourism. However, for now, I would appreciate it if my hon. friend could explain to me if there has been any new development regarding this special rebate. Will tour companies in Canada be able to claim the rebate collectively for the tourists? Will the government eliminate the $300 minimum required in order to be eligible for the rebate?

speakeroldname: Mr. Barry Moore (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member and the Liberal party do a disservice to the tourism industry by misrepresenting the impact of the GST on the tourism industry.
Every single study on this subject supports the findings of the Tourism Research Institute of the Conference Board of Canada. The facts are that tourism in Canada will continue to grow every year under the GST. After the third year of implementation, tourism will grow faster with the GST than without it. Those are the facts.

Two major reasons support these optimistic projections. First, the fact that Canada will become more competitive as a result of the GST and will allow industrial sectors to secure and maintain their share of the market. Therefore, the GST will ensure economic growth.

Second, and most important for the tourism sector, the Minister of State for Tourism working closely with the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue have designed the GST in a way that recognizes the importance of tourism to the Canadian economy.
We will have a GST rebate for international visitors which will extend to both accommodations and purchases. We are the only country to offer a rebate to international travellers for accommodations. Except for transport or air services to the continental United States, inbound and outbound international passenger transportation will also be zero rated.
March 29, 1990

Other measures being looked at to ensure the rebate system is user friendly include simplifying the administrative aspects for tour packages, as the hon. member had mentioned, and conventions where accommodation is offered as part of an all-inclusive package of services.
In addition, tourism operators will for the first time be able to claim input credits on business purchases which will reduce the price impact of the GST by 2 per cent to 3 per cent.
In designing the GST, the government has recognized tourism as an export industry, an industry with enormous
Adjournment Debate
potential for expansion and job creation. We have worked hard with the industry to ensure that tourism is in the best position to benefit from the new tax system. We have succeeded, and the hon. member should recognize that.
